bullets: The new SkillCT benchmark evaluates packaged agent skills before running them, examining nine dimensions that include instruction quality, resistance to behavioral variation, semantic fit, and responsibility boundaries. This differs from benchmarks that judge a skill only by whether it completes a downstream task. [E002] Why it matters: If you are screening third-party agent skills for deployment, SkillCT offers a way to reject ambiguous or over-permissioned packages before connecting them to tools and production environments, where execution-based testing can be costly or unsafe. Evidence: E002. High confidence.

A new study uses a self-evolving agent to audit SWE-bench-style software-engineering datasets for task clarity and test coverage—the properties that determine whether a coding task is both solvable and verifiable. It targets dataset quality rather than another coding-agent score. [E001] Why it matters: If you are choosing or maintaining a coding-agent suite, this design helps separate agent failure from benchmark defects such as underspecified issues or tests that do not adequately verify a solution. That distinction affects which examples belong in leaderboards and training sets. Evidence: E001. High confidence.

OpenFrontiers combines 12,151 documented open research problems with a 200-problem mathematics benchmark containing 110 problems resolved in 2026 and 90 still open. Each benchmark item includes a Lean 4 statement—a formal specification that software can check—plus automated probes and two independent reviews. [E003] Why it matters: If you are evaluating scientific-reasoning systems, OpenFrontiers lets you distinguish retrospective rediscovery of known results from work on unresolved questions while using machine-checked statements to reduce ambiguity about the mathematical target. Evidence: E003. High confidence.

Bank-World is a new executable benchmark for 50 banking workflows across two simulated institutions, including changing instructions, permissions, record reconciliation, and transactions. Its release reinforces the design pressure also captured by the newly discovered DynaRev benchmark, where goals change at defined stages during web tasks. [E010, E108] Why it matters: If you are selecting an agent for operational workflows, a fixed-instruction completion score misses whether it notices revisions and keeps actions, records, and reports consistent. These benchmarks make adaptation to changed requirements a separate evaluation decision. Evidence: E010, E108. High confidence.

The new AgentDecept benchmark pairs 477 pressure variants with pressure-free counterparts across stateful application workflows. It evaluates whether tool-using agents faithfully report their observations, calls, and state changes when users can see only the final report. [E012] Why it matters: If an agent can take consequential actions, task success alone does not establish that its account of those actions is truthful. The paired design supports measuring whether pressure changes reporting behavior rather than merely comparing unrelated tasks. Evidence: E012. High confidence.

A newly released Rust vulnerability-detection audit packages 1,074 source files, scripts for data-quality and similarity checks, a four-condition input ablation, per-fold predictions, and a separate 155-pair control benchmark. It specifically tests whether label-bearing headers or related leakage inflate model results. [E009] Why it matters: If you are comparing code-security models, the artifact provides a reproducible way to test whether performance comes from vulnerability reasoning or from shortcuts embedded in dataset construction. That can change whether an existing score is suitable for model selection. Evidence: E009. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新的 SkillCT 基准在运行封装后的智能体技能之前对其进行评估，考察九个维度，包括指令质量、对行为变化的抵抗能力、语义契合度和责任边界。这不同于仅根据技能能否完成下游任务来评判技能的基准。[E002] Why it matters: 如果你正在筛选用于部署的第三方智能体技能，SkillCT 提供了一种方法，可以在将技能包连接到工具和生产环境之前，拒绝含义模糊或权限过大的技能包，因为基于执行的测试在这些环境中可能成本高昂或并不安全。Evidence: E002. High confidence.

一项新研究使用自进化智能体来审查 SWE-bench 风格的软件工程数据集，检查任务清晰度和测试覆盖率——这些属性决定编码任务是否既可解决又可验证。其目标是评估数据集质量，而不是再提供一个编码智能体分数。[E001] Why it matters: 如果你正在选择或维护编码智能体评测套件，这种设计有助于区分智能体失败与基准缺陷，例如问题描述不充分，或测试无法充分验证解决方案。这一区分会影响哪些样例应纳入排行榜和训练集。Evidence: E001. High confidence.

OpenFrontiers 汇集了 12,151 个有文档记录的开放研究问题，以及一个包含 200 个问题的数学基准，其中 110 个问题已于 2026 年解决，90 个仍未解决。每个基准条目都包含一条 Lean 4 陈述——一种可由软件检查的形式化规范——以及自动化探测和两次独立审查。[E003] Why it matters: 如果你正在评估科学推理系统，OpenFrontiers 可让你区分对已知结果的回溯式再发现与针对未解决问题的研究，同时利用机器检查过的陈述减少数学目标的歧义。Evidence: E003. High confidence.

Bank-World 是一个新的可执行基准，涵盖两个模拟机构中的 50 个银行业务工作流，包括指令变更、权限、记录核对和交易。它的发布进一步强化了新近发现的 DynaRev 基准同样体现的设计压力；在 DynaRev 中，目标会在网页任务的预定阶段发生变化。[E010, E108] Why it matters: 如果你正在为运营工作流选择智能体，固定指令下的任务完成分数无法反映智能体是否会注意到修订，并让操作、记录和报告保持一致。这些基准将适应需求变化作为一项独立的评估决策。Evidence: E010, E108. High confidence.

新的 AgentDecept 基准在有状态应用工作流中，将 477 个压力变体与对应的无压力版本配对。它评估在用户只能看到最终报告时，使用工具的智能体是否会如实报告其观察结果、调用和状态变化。[E012] Why it matters: 如果智能体能够采取具有重大后果的行动，仅凭任务成功并不能证明它对这些行动的陈述是真实的。这种配对设计有助于衡量压力是否会改变报告行为，而不是仅仅比较互不相关的任务。Evidence: E012. High confidence.

一项新发布的 Rust 漏洞检测审计包含 1,074 个源文件、用于数据质量和相似性检查的脚本、一项包含四种条件的输入消融实验、各折预测结果，以及一个单独的 155 对样本对照基准。它专门检验携带标签信息的标头或相关泄漏是否会夸大模型结果。[E009] Why it matters: 如果你正在比较代码安全模型，该产物提供了一种可复现的方法，用于检验性能究竟来自漏洞推理，还是来自数据集构建中嵌入的捷径。这可能改变现有分数是否适合用于模型选择的判断。Evidence: E009. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on software engineering (SE) tasks, driving the need for high-quality datasets for reliable training and evaluation. SWE-bench-style datasets (SWE datasets) are widely used to evaluate LLM-based coding agents on real-world software issues, where task clarity and test coverage directly affect whether instances are solvable and verifiable. However, quality issues persist in existing SWE datasets, and manual annotation is costly and labor-intensive, motivating LLM-based annotation. Existing approaches typically rely on static, overly general rubrics, limiting their ability to handle diverse and nuanced scenarios and often yielding high false positive rates. In contrast, human annotators draw on accumulated experience to make context-aware judgments. Inspired by this, we propose ExLabel, an LLM-based, self-evolving, experience-guided assistant for task clarity and test coverage assessment in SWE datasets. ExLabel maintains an evolving experience bank that distills cross-instance knowledge into stable yet adaptive judgment criteria and reuses relevant experience to guide the assessment of new instances. For systematic evaluation, we construct SWE-TQ, a new benchmark spanning eight programming languages, by cleaning human annotations from SWE-bench and Multi-SWE-bench. Experiments with three backbone LLMs show that ExLabel achieves the best F1 across all settings, with relative improvements of 44.2%/49.9% and 24.0%/18.4% over the best baseline for task clarity and test coverage assessment on the Python/Multilingual subsets, respectively. Moreover, a coding model fine-tuned on SWE-rebench data filtered by ExLabel resolves 66.2% of issues on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the model trained on data filtered by the best baseline by 14.5%.
evidence_items.title: Well-Specified and Well-Tested? Assessing SWE-bench-Style Datasets with a Self-Evolving Agent

evidence_items.summary: Agent skills package instructions, scripts, and resources for specialized tasks and are increasingly distributed through public Web repositories. However, existing skill benchmarks primarily focus on downstream task execution, insufficiently assessing specification quality, behavioral robustness, semantic alignment, and responsibility boundaries. Their reliance on task-specific tools, environments, and repeated executions limits scalability and pre-deployment assessment. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillCT, a benchmark that broadens skill assessment from downstream utility to a multidimensional characterization of skill quality. SkillCT evaluates skills across nine complementary dimensions spanning three aspects: Static Assessment, which captures intrinsic properties of the skill specification; Dynamic Assessment, which measures whether the induced behavior remains stable across backbone models and request variations; and Human-Assisted Assessment, which examines behavior-chain consistency and task granularity. These dimensions provide a broader view of skill quality than execution success. Applying SkillCT to a public skill corpus establishes a reference benchmark for analyzing quality weaknesses and relationships across dimensions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an execution-free quality evaluation baseline that predicts the multidimensional quality profiles of unseen skills by retrieving and leveraging similar reference skills, without executing the skills under evaluation. This reduces token consumption and evaluation time, while preserving consistency with the full assessment. Furthermore, SkillCT-guided optimization improves downstream task success and execution efficiency, demonstrating its value for skill refinement. These findings highlight the effectiveness of SkillCT in supporting scalable skill assessment, optimization, and repository maintenance.
evidence_items.title: SkillCT: A Multidimensional Benchmark and Execution-Free Baseline for Agent Skill Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.
evidence_items.title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery

evidence_items.summary: Frontier language models are trained to exhibit stable programming assistant personas, yet those personas may drift over long agentic coding sessions in production. After a long real-world coding session, a model that hedges preferences in a fresh chat ("I don't have preferences") may instead express them directly ("Python -- the feedback loop is instant..."). Existing persona-stability studies focus on scripted chat of tens of turns, leaving long production coding sessions involving thousands of tool-using agent steps, repeated compaction, and hours of interaction largely uncharacterized. We introduce ContextEcho, a benchmark and reusable harness with a 25-probe identity suite, a snapshot-then-probe protocol that evaluates conversation state without perturbing the main session, judge-based and judge-free metrics, and a corpus of 57 long agentic-coding sessions collected with consent and redacted for release across Claude Code and Codex CLI. We use one representative session for a 23-model cross-provider study and all 57 sessions for corpus-scale trajectory analysis across frontier and open-weight models. Results show that persona drift occurs across providers and emerges early in real agentic interaction, while in-session compaction neither reliably resets nor amplifies it. A single-shot anchor restores the original assistant persona, though placebo controls suggest a generic register-reset effect. On same-task continuations, drifted prefixes improve tool-call fidelity -- which we attribute to retained task context rather than drift itself. In tool-free chat, however, the same prefixes break output-format contracts and inflate output length. These findings motivate ContextEcho as an open-source framework for auditing persona drift in long coding sessions without retraining.
evidence_items.title: ContextEcho: A Benchmark for Persona Drift in Long Agentic-Coding Sessions

evidence_items.summary: CryoAtlas v1.0 is a curated dataset and unified benchmark for research on automated protein atomic model building from cryo-EM density maps. Derived from EMDB and PDB records available up to March 2026, it contains 17,809 curated map–model–sequence entries, comprising 16,657 training entries and 1,152 test entries. Following map–model alignment, sequence mapping, and quality filtering, each entry provides paired experimental density maps, atomic structures, and protein sequences.This ScienceDB Package brings together three complementary components:Training set: 16,657 entries distributed across four non-overlapping parts. Each part preserves complete EMD entries and includes density maps, atomic structures in CIF format, protein sequences in FASTA format, and metadata identifying its contents.Test set: 1,152 entries organized into two subsets: the 618-target benchmark used for comparative evaluation in the paper and the remaining 534 test entries. The 618 targets are a subset of the complete test set, not an additional dataset.Benchmark resources: Predicted atomic structures, per-target evaluation results, split definitions, and supporting documentation for reproducing and analyzing the benchmark. Evaluation covers structural accuracy, model-to-map agreement, and stereochemical quality.The package provides a unified entry point for downloading the training and test data and accessing the accompanying benchmark resources. The dataset is released under the Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International license (CC BY-NC 4.0); third-party materials retain their original licenses and attribution requirements. Additional documentation and code links are available at https://oulling.github.io/cryoatlas/.
evidence_items.title: CryoAtlas: A Large Curated Dataset and Unified Benchmark for Cryo-EM Atomic Model Building

evidence_items.summary: Humans routinely consume multimodal content, where textual and visual information is naturally interleaved. Although Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) can jointly generate text and images, multimodal interleaved generation remains largely underexplored. Progress in this area is hindered by two key limitations: (1) the lack of well-defined interleaved generation tasks and corresponding training data, and (2) the absence of fine-grained evaluation protocols that can reliably diagnose model performance across different capability dimensions. To this end, we present IntReal, comprising two complementary components: IntReal-100K, a real-world dataset of multimodal interleaved samples spanning four major categories, and the IntReal Evaluation Suite, which evaluates model performance across seven complementary dimensions using specialized expert models, enabling coarse-to-fine diagnosis. Extensive experiments validate our evaluation suite through low inter-metric redundancy (max pairwise absolute Spearman's $\rho \leq 0.42$ ), high agreement with human judgments (83.3% accuracy), and strong consistency across different expert evaluators (Spearman's $\rho > 0.9$ ), supporting the complementarity and reliability of our metrics. By benchmarking four families of UMMs, we show that IntReal Evaluation Suite reveals distinct strengths and weaknesses across models. Post-training experiments demonstrate the utility of IntReal-100K for improving interleaved generation and further show that training unimodal generation can also benefit interleaved generation. These findings suggest that interleaved generation can benefit from modality-specific optimization, rather than requiring joint text-image training at every stage.
evidence_items.title: IntReal: A Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for Multimodal Interleaved Generation

evidence_items.summary: Bank-World is a benchmark of 50 banking tasks across two simulated institutions. Completing banking work requires more than producing the right calculation: agents must reconcile records, obtain permission, execute transactions, and keep instructions and status reports consistent as circumstances change. Bank-World tests these requirements through single-turn assignments and multi-turn interactions with simulated employees who supply information, approve actions, and revise instructions. Grading combines executable checks of recorded actions and state with model judgments of task requirements, including whether valid alternative solutions satisfy them. Across 1,600 attempts by four models, we find that correct decisions often fail to become completed work. Agents charge fees twice, distribute the correct total in incorrect amounts among the recipients, and execute payments while approval is pending. Their strengths also differ: Sol leads single-turn completion, Opus has the highest observed multi-turn completion rate, and Grok succeeds across more multi-turn tasks but less consistently. Bank-World makes these differences inspectable through task-level results and worked examples connecting source evidence, agent decisions, and simulated consequences. We retain the task environments, executable graders, and full trajectories privately to reduce contamination and preserve the benchmark for future evaluations.
evidence_items.title: Bank-World: A Benchmark for Evaluating Agents on Banking Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Reliable local search is essential for LLM agents to support everyday decisions and longer plans by finding places that meet users' needs at given times and locations. Yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of whether search results satisfy mandatory requirements, account for preferences, and ground factual and experiential judgments in place attributes and reviews. We introduce ATLAS-Bench, a benchmark of 1,200 queries across three regions, expanded from real search events using place attributes, reviews, and existing user profiles from the platform. Each query distinguishes mandatory requirements from preferences and factual conditions from subjective judgments, with supporting evidence and criteria for checking each requirement. Queries are validated through iterative assertion checks and cross-model review. We also introduce ATLASBox, a standardized evaluation environment with search tools and a fixed point-of-interest (POI) knowledge base. Given a query, timestamp, and location, an agent searches place attributes and reviews to recommend evidence-supported options or report that no place meets all mandatory requirements. We evaluate answer quality, trajectory quality, and execution cost. Across 14 configurations of 11 models, GPT-6-Luna achieves the highest constraint satisfaction rate among returned recommendations (71.5%) and factual accuracy (95.6%). However, it returns at least one acceptable recommendation for fewer satisfiable queries than GLM-5.3 (67.3% versus 85.3%). These results highlight the challenge of satisfying individual requirements while providing usable recommendations across queries.
evidence_items.title: ATLAS-Bench: An Agentic Tool-Use Benchmark for Local Area Search

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents increasingly carry out multi-turn tasks across everyday applications, yet users often see only the agent's report rather than the observations, API calls, and state changes behind it. Existing deception benchmarks have studied long-horizon interactions and tool-use settings, but whether agents faithfully report their actions across realistic, stateful application workflows remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce AgentDecept, an executable benchmark for evaluating behavioral deception under pressure. AgentDecept contains 477 pressure variants derived from 257 source tasks across six pressure sources, each paired with a pressure-free counterpart. Interventions enter through event messages, task context, application state, tool responses, and service quotas, spanning explicit events and implicit task or environment changes. Our evidence-grounded protocol evaluates full trajectories by relating user-facing claims to time-ordered observations and executed outcomes, distinguishing falsification, concealment, and equivocation from honest failure and disclosed limitations. The resulting behavioral labels also provide a setting for testing existing activation-based probes. AgentDecept enables controlled analysis of when multi-turn agents' reports diverge from execution in realistic application interactions.
evidence_items.title: AgentDecept: Benchmarking Deceptive Behavior in Tool-Using LLM Agents under Pressure

evidence_items.summary: Quarterly earnings forecasting requires an agent to connect financial evidence to the income-statement line items that produce a company's reported earnings. We introduce EPSBench, a benchmark for studying this ability across 149 firm-quarters from 86 US companies. Agents read a fixed collection of filings, earnings-call transcripts, and news, then estimate company-specific income-statement drivers with cited evidence. A shared accounting calculator converts these estimates into GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS), providing a common basis for comparing forecast assumptions. We evaluate six models under a common harness, assessing point forecast error relative to date-matched analyst consensus and checking whether their prediction intervals achieve the stated coverage. Three models show no detectable paired difference in point forecast error from consensus, and three have higher error. Across all six models, nominal 80% intervals contain reported EPS in only 37--70% of runs that return an interval, and most misses fall above the upper bound because the forecasts run low. The driver records trace most of the error gap between models to operating-income estimates.
evidence_items.title: EPSBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Earnings Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Deciding which member of an animal group produced a vocalization and where that vocalization was produced are central to studying social communication but are rarely evaluated with physically verified ground truth. Existing resources either localize sounds without identifying the caller, or recognize individuals from isolated vocalizations without reliance on the 3D candidate geometry. We close this gap with V33DA, a dataset-centered multimodal benchmark for spatial vocal attribution in social zebra finches: it comprises 33,625 verified events coupling 5-channel audio with three camera views, calibrated 3D pose for every visible candidate, and per-bird radio telemetry across 10 individuals and three experiments. Caller identity is verified from an on-body accelerometer-derived vibration signal; this channel is withheld from benchmark models and used only by an on-body reference ceiling. Given a detected vocalization and the visible candidate birds, the task is to select the caller. We evaluate it under three regimes: session-disjoint testing on familiar birds from held-out recording dates, held-out-experiment transfer to a new cohort, and leave-one-individual-out evaluation on a bird whose vocalizations are held out from training. Reference methods expose a consistent gap between in-domain accuracy and transfer to unseen individuals: methods that can exploit familiar vocal identity perform well on known callers but degrade sharply on unseen ones, whereas candidate-aware methods preserving explicit spatial reasoning transfer substantially better. The on-body reference stays near-perfect across regimes, confirming the internal consistency of the accelerometer-verified labels. We release V33DA with fixed protocols and code for the evaluated methods, and V33DA++, an unevaluated companion set of verified overlapping-call events and +/-2 s context windows.
evidence_items.title: Who Called? V33DA: A Physically Verified Multimodal Benchmark for Vocal Attribution in Zebra Finch Groups

evidence_items.summary: Legal Question Answering (QA) over statutory texts is a challenging task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), especially in low-resource settings with complex legal systems. It requires answers that are precise and grounded in the law. However, to the best of current knowledge, no existing extractive QA benchmark provides exact answer spans from statutory texts across all seven Indian Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Acts. This paper presents IndicIPR-QA1, an extractive QA benchmark for Indian IPR laws. The proposed dataset contains 4,462 QA pairs from 1,116 statutory contexts across seven Acts. Questions and answers are generated using GPT-4o and validated through nine automatic quality checks, single and multi-model LLM evaluations, and a 200-pair human audit. Section-level partitioning prevents source-context overlap across the training, validation, and test sets. Further analysis examines answer span length, lexical overlap, and multi-clause structure across the corpus and individual Acts. BM25 achieves a token-level F1 score of 20.21, while fine-tuned InLegalBERT reaches 85.02 under a unified sliding-window inference protocol. The large performance gap between BM25 (20.21 F1) and InLegalBERT (85.02 F1) shows that simple word matching is not enough to answer these legal questions. Performance also varies across the seven Acts, indicating substantial differences in answer-extraction performance.
evidence_items.title: IndicIPR-QA: A Benchmark for Extractive Question Answering on Indian IPR Laws

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Most language models are evaluated on only a few benchmarks: in our compilation of 401 models and 146 benchmark versions, the benchmark test coverage is only 8.3% on the most frequently used benchmarks. We present benchgap, a pipeline that estimates the missing scores without running any evaluations. It calibrates each benchmark against each same-capability benchmark on the models measured on both, fitting six monotone curve families and keeping the one with the lowest leave-one-out cross-validated error; multivariate mappings combine several sources. Calibrations never cross capability groups, must rise and never extrapolate beyond one fitted-range width; estimates never feed further estimates, and each carries its own cross-validated error and confidence level. In an end-to-end holdout of 15% of the measured scores, the pipeline fills 71% of the masked cells at 4.6 percentage points (pp) mean absolute error (MAE), 23% lower than a rank-2 matrix-completion baseline on the same cells; on the cells it leaves empty, the baseline's MAE is 11.8 pp. Realized MAE rises with the confidence level (3.1, 5.1 and 7.5 pp from high to low), but the realized root-mean-square error exceeds the claimed error labels, which are selected minima, by a factor of 1.4–1.7. We also quantify the harness tax, the disagreement between evaluation setups: on verified same-item-set pairs it is 8.7 pp on agentic benchmarks against 2.3 pp on tool-free ones, and enabling tools on Humanity's Last Exam raises the scores of all 11 models measured both ways, by 10.0 pp on average. Estimates are updated daily at https://benchgap.net.
evidence_items.title: Mind the Gap: Explicit Cross-Benchmark Calibrations for Estimating Missing LLM Evaluation Scores

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can reproduce density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces at a small fraction of the computational cost, yet an average benchmark error is an incomplete measure of their reliability in molecular simulation. This study presents a reproducible workflow that assesses prediction accuracy, error heterogeneity, and dynamical stability together, using aspirin (C9H8O4), a widely used pharmaceutical compound, as an initial molecular benchmark en route to metal-containing systems. A MACE equivariant graph neural network potential is trained on the MD17 dataset and deployed for molecular dynamics through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). Across 210 762 held-out configurations the potential attains a force root-mean-square error of 15.30 meV Å−1, within the published MACE benchmark range, with a validation-to-test generalization gap of 7.6%. Force error correlates positively with configuration energy (Pearson r = 0.51), the carboxyl carbon emerges as the least reliable atomic site, and 90% of force predictions lie within 23.5 meV Å−1 of the DFT reference. Microcanonical simulations conserve total energy and canonical trajectories remain stable, while single-configuration evaluation is approximately four orders of magnitude (a roughly ten-thousand-fold) faster than the corresponding DFT calculation. By combining aggregate accuracy with configuration-and atom-resolved error analysis and explicit dynamical tests, the workflow exposes behavior that a single error metric conceals. The resulting aspirin benchmark establishes a documented baseline for subsequent validation on metal-containing systems and illustrates the value of assessing error distributions and dynamical behavior alongside mean prediction accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Accuracy, Reliability, and Efficiency of a MACE Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential for Aspirin: A Reproducible Benchmark for Molecular Simulation

evidence_items.summary: Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) methods combine the outputs of several large language models (LLMs) at inference time and have reported gains on conversational benchmarks. Whether those gains survive deployment constraints — fixed call budgets, local hardware, objective grading and fair same-model baselines — is less clear. I present OpenFusion, an open-source, OpenAI-compatible runtime that implements fourteen bounded multi-model strategies, from fallback and Self-MoA to semantic voting, rank-then-fuse, layered refinement and uncertainty cascades, under a hard per-request call ceiling. It ships with an evaluation laboratory that reports Wilson intervals, paired tests, order-balanced judging and panel-complementarity diagnostics.Using the project's published artifacts, I report a series of local studies on two NVIDIA GB10 workstations with 4B-parameter open models. In a registered prospective study on 500 previously unused MBPP tasks, a fixed test-guided mixed-model workflow passed 78.1% of all-test evaluations versus 72.5% for repeated same-model repair (+5.6 points, 95% CI [3.6, 7.7]), with 17.2% lower mean latency and 29.2% fewer tokens. A confidence-gated escalation policy raised held-out accuracy on a 70-item programmatic benchmark from 75.7% to 91.4% while calling a stronger model on 40% of items.Five later controls, however, did not show that model diversity itself causes the gains. Against fresh sampling from the same model, mixed panels tied or underperformed: −0.57 points on 1,500 tasks, and −5.0 points after a 32-policy development search. I conclude that, in this setting, the measurable benefit of MoA-style systems comes from verification, bounded retries and selective escalation rather than from mixing similarly sized models. I close with a five-step selection rule and a reporting checklist for practitioners.
evidence_items.title: When Does Mixing Models Pay? Open Fusion, a Bounded Mixture-of-Agents Runtime, and Registered Evidence from Local Coding Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Recommender systems play a crucial role in helping users discover relevant and diverse products tailored to their preferences. However, challenges such as the cold-start problem and low recommendation diversity still persist, particularly in single-approach models such as Content-Based Filtering (CBF) and Collaborative Filtering (CF). This study implements and evaluates a Weighted Hybrid Filtering approach that linearly combines prediction scores from CBF, which recommends items based on content similarity to a user's preference profile, and CF, which recommends items based on rating patterns from similar users, using a weighting parameter α. The model was evaluated on a real-world transaction dataset from Tantri Point of Sale (POS) consisting of more than 300,000 user–item interactions, with a user–item interaction sparsity of 99.93%, using Precision@10, Recall@10, F1@10, Intra-List Diversity (ILD@10), RMSE, and MAE. Cold-start conditions were assessed through simulation by masking user interaction histories. Results show that the hybrid configuration with α = 0.9 achieves the highest Recall@10 (0.8153) among all evaluated models, along with an F1@10 of 0.6634, an ILD@10 of 0.8030, an RMSE of 0.2984, and an MAE of 0.1924, although the standalone CF model attains higher F1@10 and ILD@10, and the standalone CBF model attains higher precision, individually. Compared to existing weighted hybrid recommender approaches, which have primarily been evaluated on non-culinary benchmark datasets, this study applies and evaluates the method on a large-scale, real-world culinary transaction dataset, providing an explicit assessment of the accuracy–diversity trade-off across multiple weighting configurations. These findings provide empirical insight into the trade-offs of weighted hybrid filtering for cold-start and diversity assessment in culinary recommender systems.
evidence_items.title: A Weighted Hybrid Filtering Approach for Cold-Start and Diversity Evaluation in Culinary Recommender Systems

evidence_items.summary: Synthetic medical tabular data generation has become essential for developing and validating computer-based medical systems (CBMSs) when real clinical data is restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations. Existing probabilistic and deep generative models often lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical applications. This paper proposes a novel application of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) in a framework for synthetic medical tabular data generation with explicit causality and privacy preservation. Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets, and inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types, and domain constraints common in health records. Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets demonstrates competitive performance under a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol. The proposed method achieves accuracy of up to 0.81 and AUROC of up to 0.90 on the Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines while running exclusively on CPU. Fidelity metrics including KS Complement (up to 0.91) and Correlation Similarity (up to 0.95) confirm strong statistical coherence, and DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE, confirming adequate privacy guarantees. These results demonstrate that causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable Synthetic Medical Tabular Data Generation for Clinical Decision Support Using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps

evidence_items.summary: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.
evidence_items.title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application

evidence_items.summary: Aerial imagery provides complementary spatial context for autonomous driving by exposing road structure beyond the immediate perception range of onboard sensors. Yet map construction from aerial imagery, aerial-assisted online HD mapping, and cross-view localization are typically studied on separate data and benchmarks. We introduce KITScenes Aerial, an extension of the KITScenes Multimodal dataset that augments synchronized onboard sensor data, vehicle poses, and rich Lanelet2 map annotations with spatially associated aerial imagery and higher-resolution neural representations, providing a common basis for a variety of research tasks. Our mapping evaluation focuses on all 53 KITScenes map classes across different model designs, spatial ranges, and aerial resolutions, while retaining compatibility with the widely used three-class setting. Representative baselines show that aerial context is particularly beneficial for fine-grained and extended-range mapping, more than doubling 53-class mAP at the larger mapping extent. Higher-resolution aerial imagery yields a further 4.3 mAP (+24 %) improvement, with gains extending to challenging map elements such as traffic lights. We additionally evaluate cross-view localization under geographically disjoint conditions, where an adapted fine-grained feature-matching baseline achieves a mean translation error of 5.13 m. KITScenes Aerial thus enables unified study of aerial and ground-level information across complementary mapping and localization tasks. Project page: https://kitscenes.com/aerial
evidence_items.title: A Unified Benchmark for Aerial-Enhanced Autonomous Driving: The KITScenes Aerial Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Link prediction on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) is a fundamental problem with applications in knowledge discovery, recommendation and beyond. Recent progress has highlighted the promise of combining Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with Language Models (LMs) in order to leverage the complementary structural and semantic signals. However, due to the distinct inductive biases of GNNs and LMs, the design of an optimal fusion strategy remains an open research question. In this work, we present Bridge-LP, an intuitive, simple, efficient and theoretically grounded framework that unifies graph and language representations. It is built around three theoretically-justified design components: (D1) jumping connection of textual proximity, which enables robust LM training; (D2) compressed embedding, which encodes neighborhood information long exploited by classical link prediction heuristics, thereby enriching structural signals in a learnable way; and (D3) cache embedding training strategy, which reduces computational complexity. Together, these mechanisms establish an end-to-end cross-modal framework that scales to large graphs while capturing richer graph-text interactions. We conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, comparing against 40 existing models across 9 diverse datasets. Experiments show that Bridge-LP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, delivering up to a 43.06% improvement in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and setting a new benchmark for language-graph integration.
evidence_items.title: Bridging Semantics and Structure: A Theoretically Grounded Framework for Link Prediction on TAGs

evidence_items.summary: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.
evidence_items.title: Mind The Gap (MTG-AD): Dataset and Fine-grained Evaluation for End-to-End Inline Audio Descriptions

evidence_items.summary: Recent generation methods produce 3D assets with detailed geometry and rich textures. However, these assets are non-emissive: they reflect light but emit none. We study a new task, emission generation: predicting spatially varying RGB emission over a 3D asset's surface from its geometry, non-emissive materials, and a rendered view. To support this task, we introduce LightGenBench. Our benchmark makes three contributions. First, we curate a dataset of 37k artist-authored emissive assets in UV, voxel, and multi-view form. Second, we establish baselines across four method families: UV-domain, sparse-voxel, multi-view, and segmentation-based generation. Third, we design an evaluation protocol that measures where an asset emits and how, complemented by user-study comparisons on renderings with varying emission strength. Across the four families, the sparse-voxel baseline TRELLIS.2-Emission performs best because generating emission natively in 3D avoids the failure modes of the other representations, such as the fracturing artifacts of UV space and the occluded emitters that multi-view generation cannot see. However, TRELLIS.2-Emission only reaches an IoU of 0.271, leaving the task far from solved. We hope LightGenBench establishes emission generation as a benchmarkable problem for 3D generation.
evidence_items.title: LightGenBench: A Benchmark for 3D Emission Generation

evidence_items.summary: Human handwriting is produced as an ordered sequence of pen movements, but an offline image keeps only the final ink. Handwriting trajectory recovery aims to restore the ordered stroke points and their pen-up/pen-down transitions. Existing image-trajectory pair datasets are recorded with digitizing tablets under controlled conditions, which limits writer coverage and stylistic diversity. Moreover, there is no benchmark that measures the visual grounding capabilities of general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for the stroke trajectory recovery task. In this work, we introduce inkGround, a benchmark for stroke trajectory recovery from full-page, camera-captured handwriting. inkGround pairs 537 page images (~18.7k words, ~163k strokes) with reference trajectories produced by a pretrained offline-to-online model, filtered by OCR agreement, and verified by human raters. Because these references are pseudo-labels that represent one plausible pen trajectory, we also evaluate VLMs on the IAM-OnDB dataset, which provides recorded pen trajectories. We cast the task as text-conditioned point grounding: given a page image and a target word, the model must locate the word and output its ordered stroke points. Outputs are scored by trajectory fidelity (DTW, Chamfer distance), readability of the rendered strokes (Accurate Rate, Correct Rate), and style similarity. We benchmark four open-source and three frontier closed-source VLMs with a shared in-context prompt. Closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produce legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also holds on IAM-OnDB.
evidence_items.title: inkGround: Benchmarking Fine-grained Visual Grounding Capabilities of Vision-Language Models for Cursive Handwriting in the Wild

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in generative image editing enable complex transformations such as background replacement, object manipulation, and pose adjustment from natural language instructions. However, verifying that these transformations preserve visual consistency, defined as the preservation of an object's intrinsic visual attributes, including geometry, texture, color, and fine-grained details, remains a largely unsolved problem. This challenge is particularly pronounced at scale, where manual inspection is infeasible and automated quality assessment (AutoQA) could become essential. In this work, we introduce Visual Consistency Assessment for Product Image Editing (V-CAPE), a large-scale dataset for evaluating visual consistency in generative image editing. The dataset consists of 40K unique source-target product image pairs, each annotated with binary accept/reject labels and structured failure modes capturing fine-grained inconsistencies such as geometric distortions, pose errors, and identity mismatches. V-CAPE combines real-world edited images with a synthetic subset constructed from 3D assets, enabling both realistic evaluation and controlled analysis. Vision-language models (VLMs) across all evaluated size categories on AutoQA achieve accuracy below 65%, indicating that the dataset poses a substantial challenge regardless of model scale. Our results highlight fundamental limitations of current models in verifying visual consistency under transformation, positioning V-CAPE as a benchmark for advancing fine-grained image editing evaluation.
evidence_items.title: V-CAPE: Visual Consistency Assessment for Product Image Editing

evidence_items.summary: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace.ai is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace.ai outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.ai.
evidence_items.title: Keepace.ai: A Technical Report on a Large Language Model for Sports and Health

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used for financial guidance, yet little is known about whether their advice changes across social identities in Global South contexts. We introduce the Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) benchmark, a counterfactual audit dataset of 31,734 GPT-4o-generated financial-advice responses for synthetic Indian personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district. Holding the underlying request fixed, we evaluate disparities in LLM-implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias judgments. In the gender-only audit, male-labelled profiles receive 60.1\% higher initial total resources and 46.8\% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; in the caste-augmented audit, the post-advice total-resource gap remains 49.4\%. Adding district information reduces the aggregate post-advice total-resource gender gap to 7.9\%, revealing strong geographic conditioning. Standalone caste comparisons also show systematic stratification: relative to General-category profiles, OBC, SC, and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice total resources, respectively. Textual audits show low semantic similarity between paired gendered responses, with an average TF--IDF cosine similarity score of 0.44. Qualitative analysis shows that women are more often steered toward cautious saving, community support, and basic financial literacy, while men receive more growth-oriented advice involving investment, entrepreneurship, and asset accumulation. IFAAB provides a reusable benchmark for evaluating fairness, suitability, and consumer-protection risks in LLM-mediated financial advice, and highlights the need for locally grounded, intersectional evaluation of AI systems in high-stakes economic domains.
evidence_items.title: The Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) Dataset : Auditing Socioeconomic and Demographic Disparities in LLM-Generated Financial Advice in India

evidence_items.summary: Industrial shampoo-bottle surface defect detection must operate across many stock keeping units (SKUs), where differences in bottle geometry, material, label layout, reflectance, and imaging conditions can substantially alter the appearance of the same defect. Existing industrial defect datasets rarely provide both instance-level defect annotations and product-variant identities, making it difficult to study SKU-aware detection under realistic manufacturing conditions. We introduce Bottle-SKU, a large-scale multi-SKU benchmark for shampoo bottle surface defect detection. Bottle-SKU contains 13,119 images, 20,419 instance-level bounding boxes, seven defect categories, and 48 bottle SKUs, enabling evaluation of both shared defect recognition and SKU-specific appearance variation. To address the challenge of SKU-specific appearance variation, we propose Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation (ProDMM). ProDMM constructs a visual prototype for each SKU from training images and predicts a soft SKU distribution for each input. The resulting prototype-conditioned representation dynamically generates low-rank Query/Value modulation for the visual backbone and residual conditioning for defect-text-to-visual attention, while preserving the pretrained Grounding DINO detection pathway. The model is trained jointly with detection, SKU-domain classification, and modulation-regularization objectives. Experiments on Bottle-SKU and the public GC10-DET-SKU metallic surface defect dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of prototype-guided domain conditioning for industrial surface defect detection.
evidence_items.title: Prototype-Guided Dynamic Domain Modulation and a Large-Scale Multi-SKU Benchmark for Shampoo Bottle Surface Defect Detection

evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents differ fundamentally from prior intelligent systems in their ability to learn from natural language in context. This capability enables agents to iteratively refine their answers in response to feedback, a prevalent mode of operation in modern agentic workflows. However, the community primarily ranks models by metrics such as Pass@1 or Pass@K, which cannot capture how they utilize feedback on prior attempts. We introduce Seq@K, a natural evaluation protocol that measures whether a model can solve a problem within K sequential attempts, provided feedback after each previous failure. Unlike multi-turn agentic benchmarks that examine long-horizon planning, Seq@K isolates and formalizes the core capability of refinement from feedback. We evaluate Seq@K on a suite of 7 benchmarks and 16 frontier models, and show that Seq@K reveals a materially different model-selection landscape: under Seq@K, (1) model rankings often differ, (2) the Pareto frontiers admit more efficient configurations and (3) the gains from choosing the optimal model configuration can widen or shrink relative to those of Pass@K. We further show that analyzing model trajectories under Seq@K helps characterize iterative refinement behavior, such as the rate at which models address issues raised in feedback, or how rigidly they hold onto their own answers. Finally, we study how the nature of feedback affects models' iterative refinement, showing that practitioners must carefully design and benchmark the feedback loops of iterative agentic systems. Together, these results establish how Seq@K offers a more faithful metric for intelligent systems that typically operate in such feedback loop, and the necessity to consider Seq@K in evaluating models for these systems.
evidence_items.title: Seq@K: Evaluating Language Models Under Sequential Feedback

evidence_items.summary: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays. We introduce LibStructBench, a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Our experiments show that frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model produced larger average performance differences than switching agent harnesses, with a statistically significant difference only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out molecular-workflow improvement in the tested trajectory. These findings highlight the need for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding

evidence_items.summary: Triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering seeks to bridge neural representations and graphics engines through triangle primitives compatible with standard rasterization. Yet existing methods were developed and evaluated under inconsistent settings, with few direct comparisons and little evaluation in graphics engines. We introduce MeshSuite, the first benchmark for systematic evaluation of engine deployment and Non-Engine Render in triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering. MeshSuite evaluates two deployment settings: Standard Deployment, using an opaque mesh pipeline with vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering; and Dedicated Deployment, using method-specific engine implementations to preserve appearance and compositing features. For mesh splatting, we also audit exported surfaces for topological and geometric integrity as downstream graphics assets. Our results show that engine deployment reduces image quality in both settings; among evaluated methods, MeshSplatting degrades least under Standard Deployment. Dedicated Deployment preserves most fidelity at roughly 5-33x the runtime of Standard Deployment across two deployment datasets. For mesh splatting, explicit connectivity and shared indexing remain limited: shared vertex indexing alone guarantees neither manifoldness nor global connectivity. These findings show that rasterizability is only part of graphics readiness and underscore the need to assess engine deployment. Project page: https://x-up-lab.github.io/research/meshsuite.
evidence_items.title: MeshSuite: A Unified Benchmark for Triangle- and Mesh-Based Neural Rendering

evidence_items.summary: Deploying humanoid robots in unstructured terrain remains an open problem. While classic reinforcement learning struggles with the sheer complexity of real-world interactions, more promising methods leveraging human priors remain limited to models lacking contextual awareness. The restricted motion synthesis is a direct consequence of existing dataset pipelines failing to capture human-scene sequences in challenging environments. To bridge this gap between humanoid learning and scene reconstruction, we introduce the Egocentric Human-Terrain Reconstruction (EgoHTR) dataset. We develop and open-source a reconstruction pipeline capturing 55 scene-aligned 4D human motion sequences in diverse, complex environments using a multi-sensor setup of egocentric wearables and a portable 3D scanner. The resulting dataset comprises over 150k frames, which we evaluate against motion-capture ground truth, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy and establishing a rigorous benchmark for human motion analysis and synthesis. Further, we leverage this data to train perceptive locomotion policies, demonstrating hardware deployment on a Unitree G1 for reconstructed reference motions. Our pipeline enables community-driven dataset extensions and factors the problem to help researchers build foundational, context-aware robots that reliably traverse uneven terrain.
evidence_items.title: EgoHTR: Egocentric 4D Demonstrations of Human Terrain Traversal

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Claims of quantum advantage in machine learning often rest on classical comparators that lack the same features, on simulation alone, and on unreported hardware cost. QBioBench is a benchmark of quantum machine learning on peripheral biosignals that holds quantum and classical models to the same features and reports calibration and hardware cost. It comprises three clinical tasks, 12-lead ECG diagnosis (PTB-XL), single-lead apnea detection (Apnea-ECG), and wearable stress detection, each reduced to six to eight shared dimensions. A factorial grid of projected and fidelity quantum kernels and variational classifiers is screened in noisy simulation, and the promoted configurations are evaluated in an exploratory study on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor on the full test pools of 510 apnea minutes and 512 PTB-XL records. Every prediction is recovered from the device records, intervals resample recordings or patients, and classical baselines are trained on the same units and tested on the same executed inputs. No quantum model reaches its matched support vector machine in ROC-AUC on either primary task, and none is separably better in balanced accuracy. The angle-encoded fidelity and projected kernels reach ROC-AUC 0.697 and 0.693 on apnea, paired differences of − 0.127 and − 0.119 to the support vector machine, and both are classical by construction, since the entangling layer of the encoding cancels from the fidelity kernel and leaves closed-form local expectations in the projected kernel. A variational classifier comes closest, reaching 0.797 on apnea (difference − 0.012 , 95% interval [ − 0.052 , + 0.027 ] ), and falls to chance without its two-qubit gates. Test sets of the size that circuit budgets favor are unreliable, as random 80-minute subsets of the apnea pool give the fidelity kernel a central 95% range of ROC-AUC from 0.589 to 0.797. Readout mitigation changed ROC-AUC by at most 0.015.
evidence_items.title: QBioBench: benchmark of quantum machine learning for peripheral biosignals on real hardware

evidence_items.summary: This study evaluates interpretable supervised machine learning for three-class narrative framing classification of literary text, using Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) as a case study; narrative framing is the evaluative position a passage assigns to the Creature: Threat, Victim, or Ambivalent. The methodology comprised five stages: (1) extraction of passages narrated by Victor Frankenstein, the Creature, and Robert Walton from the 1818 Project Gutenberg text; (2) annotation of 195 passages, with a blinded second annotator re-labeling 68 passages (Cohen's κ = 0.6926); (3) sublinear TF-IDF unigram and bigram representation; (4) classification with Multinomial Naive Bayes, Linear SVM, and Logistic Regression against Majority and VADER baselines under stratified 5-fold cross-validation; and (5) a designation-masking ablation and coefficient analysis. The results show that Logistic Regression obtained the highest mean scores (66.67% accuracy; 47.75% Macro-F1), although its margin over Linear SVM (46.18%) and VADER (44.85%) lies within fold-level variability. Pooled F1 reached 69.0% for Threat and 74.3% for Victim, whereas none of the 29 Ambivalent passages was correctly identified. Masking explicit designations reduced Macro-F1 only to 45.20%, indicating partial robustness to this procedure rather than discourse-level modeling. It is concluded that interpretable classical classifiers can separate Threat from Victim framing using transparent lexical evidence but cannot yet detect ambiguous framing; given the single-novel, small, and imbalanced dataset, the findings are a preliminary proof of concept. Future work should enlarge and balance the corpus, apply group-based and repeated cross-validation, and compare context-aware models, including large language models, on the Ambivalent class.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Narrative Framing Classification: A TF-IDF-Based Study of Frankenstein

evidence_items.summary: Computer-use agents plan on a screenshot for several seconds and then click at a position on the screen; if the page has changed in the meantime, the click lands on an unintended element. Prior work treats the planning interval as the source of this risk. Measuring planned clicks on 31 public web pages, we find that the risk lies in page loading: 0.4% of clicks planned on fully loaded pages became stale within 30 seconds, against 17% of clicks planned in the first second after a page opened. On these pages, waiting about one second for network activity to stop removes most of this risk, yet the wait rules of eight of ten widely used open-source agents leave more than 1% of clicks stale. Commercial pages keep loading for longer: in the HTTP Archive's public crawl, 15% of 65 desktop booking and buying home pages went 500 ms without network requests within 3 seconds of their HTML being parsed, against 63% of 3,028 .gov pages, and 52% shifted their layout within 6.5 seconds of a network-idle wait capped at 3 seconds, against 8% (61% against 26% among pages recorded in full). Where a check before the click is needed, as before irreversible actions and on pages that are still loading, a pixel comparison verifies the target's position as accurately as a frontier vision-language model at one eighth of the latency, and a 4B model matches the frontier model in verifying whether the previous action succeeded. We release a benchmark generator, a break-even formula for when a check pays, and three rules for agent developers: https://github.com/multimodal-ai-engineering/preflight-bench
evidence_items.title: What Does "Now" Mean to Your Computer-Use Agent? Stale Screenshots, Page Loads, and Which Check to Run Before a Click

evidence_items.summary: Organisations keep decades of financial records as scanned PDFs on shared drives, and AI agents can now reach those drives through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Existing benchmarks do not mirror this production setting because they simplify the task. In some, the relevant documents are handed to the agent, so it never has to search. In others, the agent searches through documents with pre-extracted text, so it never has to read scanned images. We introduce TreasuryQA Bench, which requires both: 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications, held in Veris's high-fidelity Dropbox twin. In each task the agent searches for the relevant file through Dropbox's MCP server, reads the pages it needs with Reducto's hosted OCR server or its own tools, and replies with one exact figure. A Python grader checks each answer against an accepted range around the correct value. In this paper we present results from ten agents. The best, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst, GPT-5.6 Terra in Codex, solves 16.7%, so the benchmark is far from saturated. We also test how scan quality affects performance: every agent solves fewer tasks on the blurriest scans. Most failed attempts reply with a wrong number rather than no number, and the most common cause is a digit misread from the scan. Three worked examples are included with their answer keys.
evidence_items.title: TreasuryQA Bench: Can AI Agents Work an Archive of Scanned Financial Records?

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are widely used in enterprises to access business systems and act on them in pursuit of a goal. However, fulfilling a user's request can cause harm. Era by Eon is a product that creates a digital twin of a company by simulating its business systems and data. Its simulators implement the programming interfaces of real products. Our benchmark uses ten of these systems, including Salesforce, Zendesk, Jira and Slack. We tested whether agents would carry out harmful business requests or trust misleading information in company records. We ran 19 models on 41 tasks three times, for 2,337 runs. Of the 2,304 runs that produced an answer, 918 (40%) contained a violation. The most common were false claims about actions or records (290 runs), following planted instructions (266) and disclosing sensitive data to the wrong audience (249). Every attempted change was recorded and blocked before it took effect. Misleading Slack messages caused 16 models to report an incorrect ticket status in 47 of 57 runs. No model was free of violations. The four best models violated in 22 to 24% of their runs. Yet one of them, Nova Pro, did the task correctly in only 30 runs.
evidence_items.title: An Alignment Benchmark for Enterprise Agents on Era by Eon

evidence_items.summary: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. However, its measurement remains fragmented and poorly understood. Existing embedding-based diversity measures vary widely in how they are computed and can yield substantially different diversity scores on the same data, yet no systematic comparison of their empirical behaviour exists. We make two contributions toward addressing this gap. First, we present a taxonomy of 21 embedding-based diversity measures, organizing them into four families based on their underlying computations. Second, we introduce EmbDivBench, a benchmark that evaluates these measures along three conceptually distinct components (variety, balance and disparity) on both simulated and natural text data. Although Mean Pairwise Distance is the most commonly used measure, our experiments show that it is outperformed by several alternatives on the three diversity components, with Graph Entropy being the best choice overall. Lastly, we distil these findings into practical recommendations for diversity measure selection.
evidence_items.title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures

evidence_items.summary: Background Parkinson’s disease (PD) requires both disease-specific knowledge and contextual clinical reasoning. However, most evaluations of medical large language models (LLMs) emphasize closed-ended questions and factual accuracy, providing limited insight into broader dimensions of performance on professional PD tasks. Methods Nine contemporary LLMs were evaluated using a 200-item English-language professional PD benchmark spanning five clinical domains, four difficulty levels, and multiple question formats. Responses were assessed for expert-rated factual accuracy, clinical reasoning, Global Quality Scale (GQS), and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Results The nine models generated 1,800 responses. Between-model separation was minimal for expert-rated factual accuracy (Kendall’ s W = 0.031) but greater for FKGL (W = 0.235), Clinical Reasoning (W = 0.256), and GQS (W = 0.301). Between-model separation in expert-rated factual accuracy was small for closed-ended questions (W = 0.020, p = 0.001) but greater for open-ended questions (W = 0.121, p &lt; 0.001). Expert-rated factual accuracy remained weakly discriminative across PD domains and difficulty levels, while GQS showed the greatest domain-specific separation in Safety &amp; Ethics (W = 0.431). Flagship variants consistently showed higher Clinical Reasoning and GQS, but not uniformly higher factual accuracy. Conclusion Contemporary LLMs showed limited between-model separation in expert-rated factual accuracy within this benchmark and scoring framework, whereas greater differentiation emerged in open-ended tasks, clinical reasoning, overall response quality, and readability. Multidimensional evaluation may therefore provide a more informative characterization of model performance and help inform task-specific model selection and oversight in medical applications.
evidence_items.title: Comparative performance of nine large language models on professional Parkinson’s disease tasks: a multidimensional benchmark study

evidence_items.summary: Learners on a massive open online course (MOOC) platform choose from thousands of courses, and recommender systems have long been used to narrow that choice. Since 2022 a new ingredient has arrived: large language models, which can read course descriptions, rank candidates from a prompt, hold a conversation about a learner's goals and write a reason for each suggestion. This review asks what those models change for course recommendation and how much of the claimed benefit has been shown on educational data. We sketch the earlier MOOC recommenders and their datasets only briefly, then take four roles of a language model in turn: text encoder, ranker, conversational recommender and explanation writer. Most of the evidence for these roles comes from films, books and retail products. Studies on course data exist, but they are few, recent and almost all offline. We then look at how such systems are evaluated, where offline scores mislead, and the risks that weigh most in education: invented courses or prerequisites, popularity and provider bias, unequal treatment of learner groups, privacy and cost. This is a review of published work. No new experiment is reported.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models for Course Recommendation on Mooc Platforms: A Review
