evidence_items.summary: We present ScaffoldForge, a 3D conditional diffusion framework for the generative design of bone scaffolds. ScaffoldForge maps a set of standardized trabecular descriptors (bone volume fraction BV/TV, trabecular thickness Tb.Th, trabecular spacing Tb.Sp, trabecular number Tb.N, connectivity density Conn.D, structure model index SMI, degree of anisotropy DA, and permeability k) to a 3D scaffold architecture in a single forward pass. A multi-objective conditioning mechanism couples these descriptors through adaptive instance normalization, and a physics-constrained loss adds empirical penalties for stiffness, manufacturing feasibility, and perfusion, evaluated on the denoiser’s reconstruction of the clean scaffold so that the penalties carry gradient. To address the scarcity of paired geometry–property data, we describe a procedural pipeline whose generated scaffolds reproduce the morphometric distributions of real micro-CT references. In an in silico evaluation on three benchmark datasets, ScaffoldForge attains an estimated 56.6 MPa compressive strength (8.2% over topology optimization; paired t-test, p = 0.043, n = 5 seeds) and reduces design-time cost from 8,400–12 seconds per design, a 700× speedup. Generated structures are diverse rather than memorized, and morphometric accuracy holds across all seven shape descriptors. Three analyses probe the reliability of these results given the small training corpus. Equivalence testing replaces the earlier argument from non-significant difference tests: the procedural and real descriptor distributions are equivalent at a medium margin of 0.5 standard deviations for all seven descriptors, but the 50 available real reference volumes cannot establish equivalence at a strict 0.3-standard-deviation margin for five of them. A classifier two-sample test shows that generated scaffolds retain a measurable but shrinking signature of the procedural generator. Enlarging the corpus from 250 to 2,050 scaffolds leaves in-distribution accuracy nearly unchanged while reducing the cross-dataset descriptor error on unseen anatomy from 0.079 to 0.058, which localizes the cost of the small corpus in generalization rather than in fit. We further illustrate a CT-to-scaffold pipeline for personalized generation. All results are computational; physical, biological, manufacturing, and regulatory validation remain future work.
evidence_items.title: ScaffoldForge: Bioinspired generative design of 3D-printed bone scaffolds via conditional diffusion for large segmental bone defect reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) appear to represent and reason about a large range of phenomena. In particular, recent studies have examined whether LLMs can accurately reason about causation. One of the most commonly used benchmarks for evaluating formal causal reasoning in LLMs is CLadder, a framework for procedural generation of benchmark data sets that was released in 2023. Experiments with CLadder appear to indicate that LLMs can perform formal causal reasoning in a large percentage of generated examples. In this paper, we examine what can be reliably inferred when LLMs perform well on test sets produced by CLadder. We identify several examples of superficial and highly predictive patterns that the CLadder generator embeds in data sets it generates. We find that even simple models such as random forests perform well on CLadder-generated data sets after training on a sample of generated data. We also find that the performance of many commercial LLMs on CLadder test sets is extremely brittle and that removing large sections of the text that are critical for formal causal reasoning has almost no effect on performance. Given these results, the most likely hypothesis for the strong performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on CLadder is that they are exploiting superficial patterns learned from exposure to training data from the generator. Any inference that LLMs are exhibiting more complex causal reasoning must rule out this hypothesis.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Causal Reasoning in LLMs: A Case Study in the Challenges of Procedural Generation

evidence_items.summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks

evidence_items.summary: This technical report details the numerical setup, validation, and coupled structural-thermal analysis of a dual-layer concentric high-pressure vessel. The internal liner chamber is configured under a severe pressure load of 200 bar (20 MPa). The assembly utilizes an inner structural core engineered from precipitation-hardened AISI 630 Stainless Steel paired with an outer thermal-insulating shield composed of technical ceramic Aluminum Titanate (Al2TiO5). Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) was employed to map the internal aerodynamics and thermal fields under an external environment temperature of 45°C. The physical parameters were successfully compiled and mapped to a Finite Element Analysis (FEA) model to evaluate structural viability and safe stress thresholds.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract: Remote monitoring of free-ranging wildlife and anti-poaching surveillance across vast ecosystems are fundamentally constrained by environmental clutter, dynamic vegetation, camouflage, and the spatial rigidity of ground-based camera traps. Inspired by the hunting strategies of birds of prey, we present trACT (temporal revelation Airborne Camera Trap), an autonomous aerial sensing framework that converts consumer drones into mobile, high-altitude camera traps. By unifying Temporal Max Pooling (TMP) –a low-overhead signal processing method that extracts hidden motion trails across rolling integration windows– with self-supervised Noise-Contrastive Estimation (NCE), trACT reliably distinguishes subtle animal or person movement from background thermal noise and wind-induced foliage motion. To overcome mechanical and computational latency (946ms loop turnaround), the system combines motion prediction with automated gimbal zoom verification and multi-target balancing. Field validation across temperate forest, urban canopy surveillance grounds, and rainforest habitats demonstrates that trACT bridges wide-area aerial scanning with precise target verification, elevating a recall of 83.8%-87.6% when paired with AI vision-reasoning. Temporal Max Pooling Results:  https://zenodo.org/records/23079962 Data S1. The dataset contains all trACT verification images for the wildlife monitoring experiments (both before and after outlier removal and visual reasoning-based species classification) along with manually selected and classified ground truth images. The data are organized by flight (date and flight number). A companion Python script for outlier removal and species classification is also provided.   Data S2. The dataset contains all trACT verification images for the surveillance experiments (both before and after outlier removal) along with manually curated ground truth images.
evidence_items.title: trACT: temporal revelation Airborne Camera Trap

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Radiology reports serve as the definitive clinical record of imaging diagnoses, with their accuracy being directly critical to patient safety. However, amid escalating workloads, manual review remains inadequate for capturing subtle errors in reports on a large scale. Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable promise in medical text processing, previous studies have predominantly been confined to radiology report text from a single imaging modality or datasets with synthetic errors. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, accuracy, and generalizability of general-purpose LLMs for quality assurance of radiology report text from multiple imaging modalities (x-ray, computed tomography [CT], and magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]), multi-anatomical regions, and multicenter clinical settings, with head-to-head comparisons conducted against radiologists of varying seniority. Methods Radiology report texts from 3 aforementioned imaging modalities and 5 anatomical regions (head, chest, abdomen, spine, and knee) were retrospectively collected from center 1 (March 2025-May 2025) and reviewed using a clinician-annotated 5-category error taxonomy (type 1: interpretive; type 2: factual). Five LLMs (Qwen3, GPT-5.4 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Llama 4, and DeepSeek-V3.1) were benchmarked on 10,000 randomly selected reports, and the best-performing model was evaluated on the full cohort. A blinded head-to-head comparison with 3 radiologists (3-10 years of experience) used a modality-stratified, error-enriched challenge set. The radiologists subsequently rated the model-generated explanations using a 5-point Likert scale. Cross-center performance was evaluated in an independent external cohort. The same 2 senior radiologists labeled reports from both centers using the same protocol, resolving disagreements by consensus.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Assisted Radiology Report Quality Assurance: Real-World Multicenter Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Scientific evidence is predominantly communicated through unstructured articles, while many downstream workflows require structured representations of study populations, variables, methods, and quantitative findings. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising route toward automating this transformation, yet their reliability in constructing schema-constrained evidence records from parsed scientific full texts remains insufficiently understood. Evidence synthesis is a representative use case in which systematic reviews and meta-analyses require accurate, structured study information before quantitative integration can begin. We present a schema-grounded, tiered evaluation framework for structured scientific evidence extraction that increases task difficulty from single-entity identification to relational tuples and corpus-level statistical tasks. We evaluate frontier commercial and open-weight models across five scientific domains under a stricter multi-level assessment protocol, complemented by human validation of model-based judging and process-level inspection of intermediate reasoning for statistical tasks. Results reveal a clear pattern: models perform substantially better on low-complexity extraction tasks than on tasks requiring correct bindings among entities, numerical values, and methodological attributes. Intermediate-step analysis further indicates error amplification under exact downstream aggregation, where small upstream errors often prevent correct final outputs. Scaling model size yields uneven gains and does not remove these weaknesses. These findings show that recent advances have not resolved the fundamental challenges of structured scientific evidence extraction. We provide a reusable query suite and diagnostic evaluation framework to support future fine-grained benchmarks and more rigorous assessment of models for evidence-intensive scientific workflows.
evidence_items.title: Diagnosing the limits of large language models for structured scientific evidence extraction

evidence_items.summary: The expertly rectified extraction of cropland parcel boundaries is a critical basis for precision agriculture deployment and land resource management. However, the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality, cross-regional reference datasets limits the generalizability of deep learning models. To address this data bottleneck, we created a standardized, multi-source cropland parcel boundary benchmark dataset. The collection, which covers Europe (Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain) and Asia (Central China), encompasses over 180,000 expert-rectified parcels, with average parcel sizes ranging from 0.05 to 10 hectares and spatial resolutions spanning 0.2 to 10 m. Based on this dataset, we evaluated nine representative deep learning models belonging to three architectural paradigms (edge detection, multi-task semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation) and analyzed the effects of spatial resolution, parcel scale, and topographic relief on extraction accuracy. The experimental results indicate the following: (1) Spatial resolution exerts a non-linear influence on boundary extraction fidelity, where some medium-resolution data conditions (such as 4.8 m imagery in large-scale fields) retained competitive boundary extraction performance for certain models. (2) Even small but regular parcels of merely 0.22 hectares can be extracted with high accuracy, achieving a maximum F1 score of 86.58%. (3) Topographic variations lead to contrasting model performance. In plain and hilly terrain, multi-task semantic segmentation models exhibit obvious advantages. BsiNet yields the highest F1 score of 86.58%, but this value drops to 36.56% in complex mountainous regions. By comparison, edge detection models perform better in mountainous areas, where RCF attains the maximum F1 of 70.85%.
evidence_items.title: A Multi-Source Benchmark Dataset for Deep Learning-Based Cropland Parcel Boundary Extraction

evidence_items.summary: Abstract While deep learning has significantly advanced image reconstruction of electrical capacitance tomography (ECT), most public datasets retain only capacitance vectors and permittivity distributions and do not expose the excitation-wise electric potential field, a physical intermediate in the forward mapping. To address this, we present an electric-potential-augmented ECT benchmark dataset generated via a COMSOL–MATLAB pipeline for a fixed eight-electrode sensor. The dataset comprises 20 000 randomized samples across four typical flow-pattern families. Alongside conventional capacitance vectors and permittivity images, each sample preserves eight spatially registered full-field potential maps. Governing equations and field-perturbation visualizations characterize the relation between potential and dielectric structure. As an initial use of this physical information, we introduce potential-field intermediate supervision to guide representation learning in simple forward and inverse models. Under sample-disjoint independent and identically distributed (IID) and fully held-out two-bar out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, potential supervision reduces forward capacitance-prediction mean squared error (MSE) by 56.8% and 74.6%, respectively, relative to a structure- and capacity-aligned control. In an exploratory forward experiment, a low-weight partial differential equation residual yields 5.3%–8.3% lower mean potential-prediction MSE. For inverse reconstruction, the simple model reduces mean MSE by 14.3% and 3.0% on IID and OOD data, respectively, relative to the same control. The more modest inverse gains are consistent with the difficulty of recovering dense potential maps from limited capacitance measurements. These results provide initial controlled evidence for the value of potential-field supervision.
evidence_items.title: An electric-potential-augmented benchmark dataset for electrical capacitance tomography: electric-potential supervision for future physics-guided learning

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Specialist agents such as Biomni, STELLA and ToolsGenie wrap large language models in curated tools and multi-agent scaffolds for bioinformatics. We asked whether a current frontier model in an off-the-shelf coding harness still needs them. Claude Opus 5.5 (high effort) in Claude Code solved all 244 tasks of PromptBio-Bench, whose free-form output files are scored against expert references. It was run with and without 667 bioinformatics Agent Skills (bioSkills, ClawBio). Under the original evaluation framework with GPT-5.6 judges, Claude with skills completed every task and reached 0.869 accuracy, against 0.758 for Biomni and ToolsGenie and 0.717 for STELLA (paired McNemar p ≤ 2 × 10−4). Its failures exposed eleven evaluator defects and several incorrect reference answers. With these defects fixed, Claude reached 0.918 to 0.926 with skills and 0.873 to 0.902 without, across GPT and Claude judges that agreed on 95 to 98% of tasks. Skills added only 2.5 to 4.5 points, yet transcripts showed the agent never invoked one; the gap traces to run-to-run variation in a few judgement calls. Of the 18 tasks still failed, 11 trace to defective references or unstated settings, and most of the rest are defensible alternatives to the reference. A general-purpose frontier model now matches or exceeds purpose-built bioinformatics agents on realistic analyses; benchmark reliability, not agent capability, has become the main limit on measuring progress.
evidence_items.title: The Generalist Strikes Back:\\A General LLM Agent Outperforms Specialist Bioinformatics Agents on Free-Form, End-to-End Benchmark Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Background. Portable near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy has been proposed as an adjunct for skin-lesion triage, and the public NIR-SC-UFES dataset has made in vivo NIR spectra of skin lesions available for machine-learning benchmarks. Two questions that bear on how such benchmarks should be read have received little attention: how results depend on the labeling of actinic keratosis (ACK), a pre-malignant lesion that the dataset convention places in the non-cancer group, and whether the wavelengths that classifiers rank as important are stable enough to support spectroscopic interpretation. Methods. We analyzed the original NIR-SC-UFES file (714 in vivo spectra, 331 patients, 908-1676 nm, 125 points; MicroNIR Pro 1700). After standard normal variate (SNV) normalization, five classifiers (RBF support vector machine, logistic regression, random forest, PLS-DA and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network) were evaluated with nested cross-validation in which every patient was confined to a single outer fold (5 outer x 3 inner folds; hyperparameters selected on inner folds only). We compared four labelings of ACK and two pairwise tasks, measured the stability of band importance over 60 patient-level bootstrap resamples, and tested the effect of removing top-ranked, random or contiguous bands. Results. On the standard binary task (647 spectra, 319 patients) the SVM reached macro-F1 0.764 +/- 0.005, balanced accuracy 0.772 +/- 0.006 and ROC-AUC 0.842 +/- 0.006 (mean +/- SD over five repetitions of the outer split); sensitivity was 0.72 and specificity 0.83. Logistic regression, random forest and the 1D-CNN were within the fold-to-fold variability of the SVM (paired Wilcoxon test, SVM vs. CNN, p = 0.63; patient-bootstrap 95% CI of the AUC difference -0.006 to 0.064). The labeling of ACK changed performance more than the choice of classifier did: macro-F1 was 0.764 with ACK as non-cancer, 0.743 with ACK excluded and 0.677 with ACK counted as positive. ACK was more separable from malignant lesions (AUC 0.876) than benign lesions were (AUC 0.813), while benign lesions and ACK were only moderately separable (AUC 0.794). Band importance was unstable at the level of single bands (mean Jaccard overlap of the top-10 bands 0.34; mean Spearman correlation 0.51), yet the top-ranked band fell within 908-1051 nm in 59 of 60 resamples. Removing the top 5-20 ranked bands lowered macro-F1 by at most 0.016, and removing 20 contiguous bands around the top band by 0.028; removing random bands had no effect. Conclusions. On this cohort, classical and deep classifiers perform similarly under nested patient-level validation, while the definition of the non-cancer class has a larger effect. The informative spectral region is reproducible, but individual band rankings are not, so single-wavelength chemical assignments should be avoided. Studies on NIR-SC-UFES should state how ACK is labeled and should report band importance across resamples.
evidence_items.title: Actinic keratosis labeling and single-band instability in near-infrared spectroscopy of skin cancer: a nested, patient-level re-analysis

evidence_items.summary: Lunar orbital missions, such as Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Kaguya/SELENE, Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory, and Lunar Prospector, among others, provide rich multi-instrument observations, but their heterogeneity in sampling, projection, and conventions limits reproducible machine learning (ML). We introduce SomBench, a unified, spatially-aligned, ML-ready lunar dataset aggregating 30+ co-registered layers from ten instruments across four missions, spanning 1 meter to 20 kilometer/pixel and covering 82 degree latitude in 90 Lunar Transverse Mercator zones with two polar stereographic caps. An image-anchored tiling pipeline yields pretraining-ready multimodal tile views with leakage-safe splits, distributed as netCDF with Parquet catalogs. An application benchmark suite spans impact processes, volcanic history, and polar volatiles. Baseline experiments with ResNet-50 and SwinV2-B models confirm that each benchmark task is learnable from the released inputs, establishing reference points for future model development.
evidence_items.title: SomBench: Benchmark Dataset for Advancing Machine Learning in Lunar Science

evidence_items.summary: The union of Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming the way Computer-Aided Design (CAD) and Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) systems are used in the Industry 4.0 production process. Based on the PRISMA 2020 reporting framework (Page et al., 2021), this report is a systematic literature review on the intelligent integration of CAD and CAM technologies in adaptive manufacturing. Based on a structured search of major scientific databases, a curated list of peer-reviewed studies was analysed thematically to address five research questions related to designing with AI, toolpath optimisation using AI, IoT/IIoT architectures for real-time adaptive control, interoperability standards and barriers to AI adoption in specific sectors. AI models, especially deep learning, graph neural networks and reinforcement learning, have led the way in recent research and development on automatic feature recognition and toolpath generation, while digital twins, edge computing and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) sensor networks are more and more being used to implement predictive maintenance and closed-loop adaptive control in the shop floor. The design phase is also starting to change with Generative AI to enable manufacturability constraints to be built in earlier in the CAD process. The literature, however, shows that there are still significant gaps that need to be addressed: AI models deployed outside of the simulation environment are not adaptable in real-time, training datasets are not standardized and openly shared, and there are interoperability protocols that are still quite disjointed, and resources for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) looking to use these technologies are still limited. To situate these gaps in a particular developing-economy context, this review is also supplemented by a series of recently published empirical studies. The review suggests that interoperability standards, Human Safety for Industry 5.0 design principles, cybersecurity, and sustainable practice are the key factors that need to be coordinated for the intelligent CAD/CAM-IoT integration to be fully realised, and it presents a roadmap of future research directions for adaptive and connected manufacturing ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: INTELLIGENT CAD/CAM INTEGRATION FOR ADAPTIVE MANUFACTURING: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF AI AND IOT FRAMEWORKS IN INDUSTRY 4.0

evidence_items.summary: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.
evidence_items.title: A-RSI: Adaptive Task Refresh for Zero-Data Multimodal Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly formalized as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), in which an agent maximizes expected reward while keeping its expected cumulative cost below a specified safety bound. Existing safe RL benchmarks predominantly report whether an algorithm is safe on average, following this expectation-based guarantee. We argue that this convention is insufficient to reliably characterize an algorithm's true safety: it fails to capture how often and how severely the safety bound is violated, whether this holds consistently across tasks and safety bounds, and whether training-time behavior is representative of behavior of the final converged policy. Therefore, we introduce (i) evaluation metrics for safe RL that address each of these concerns and in addition allow for aggregation across tasks and safety bounds. We furthermore define (ii) a safety tier system to systematically categorize and compare algorithms in terms of safety and reliability at both training and for a final policy. Using this framework, we provide (iii) an empirical safety evaluation across multiple safety navigation tasks. Our results show that aggregate metrics, distributional reporting, and task- and safety bound-specific results each reveal information the other metrics cannot. We therefore recommend reporting all three jointly, rather than compressing this information into a single value, as is common practice. We provide SafeRLEval, an open-source evaluation suite to support the reliable characterization of safety in future safe RL research.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation Metrics for Safe Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Chemical structures are published as images, which makes them inappropriate for database indexing, structure search and computational reuse. Recognition tools recover them after publication and cannot restore what the rendering discarded. BChemXtract is an open-source Java library that extracts structures directly from the ChemDraw CDX and CDXML files authors already submit. It separates chemical fragments from annotations, expands abbreviations from a curated lookup table and converts the structures with the Chemistry Development Kit into standard identifiers. In the Beilstein Journals the extracted structures are validated by hand, embedded in the article metadata as Schema.org JSON-LD and deposited in PubChem. Volume 20 of the Beilstein Journal of Organic Chemistry (BJOC), 2993 figures and schemes, yielded 23,320 structures with InChIs in under two minutes. On a 225-file benchmark 98.2% of unique substances got a valid InChI, against 14.2% with Open Babel. MIT licence, with a web application and the benchmark corpus. Library: github.com/beilstein-institut/bchemxtract Web application: cheminfo.beilstein.org/bchemxtract
evidence_items.title: BChemXtract: Automated Extraction and FAIRification of Chemical Structures from Scientific Publications

evidence_items.summary: SGCFS and Encoder Booster: code for leakage free, shift aware cloud intrusion detection   This archive contains the Python code that accompanies the manuscript “Stability Guided Feature Consensus and Calibrated Encoder Boosting for Leakage Free, Shift Aware Intrusion Detection in Cloud Networks” by Muhammad Musab Khan Sherwani and Muhammad Zunnurain Hussain.   The software implements three components. First, SGCFS, a stability guided consensus feature selector that is fitted on training days only. It keeps features that mutual information, Spearman correlation and ANOVA F scores endorse repeatedly across resampled subsets, and then removes redundant features. Second, an encoder booster that feeds a small neural bottleneck embedding together with the selected features into gradient boosted trees, with isotonic calibration on a validation day and a decision threshold fixed at a target false positive rate. Third, an evaluation protocol with a temporal train, validation and test split, a shifted second environment, bootstrap and paired bootstrap intervals, an ablation study, a sensitivity analysis, a leakage comparison and resource measurements.   The code works on the public CSECICIDS2018 dataset (Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity and the AWS Open Data registry). It also includes a synthetic flow generator for smoke testing.   Contents: src/ holds the data loader, the selectors (Corr, IG, Chi2, the stacked filter baseline and SGCFS), the models, the experiment, sensitivity and leakage scripts, the figure script and the manuscript builder. results/ holds the stored result files and figures/ the figures used in the paper. The README gives the exact commands to reproduce every table and figure.   Requirements: Python 3.10 or later, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, SciPy, Matplotlib and python-docx. XGBoost and TensorFlow are optional.   The dataset is not redistributed here and must be downloaded from its original source.
evidence_items.title: Stability Guided Feature Consensus and Calibrated Encoder Boosting for Leakage Free, Shift Aware Intrusion Detection in Cloud Networks

evidence_items.summary: Visual commissions require image agents to integrate heterogeneous source materials, preserve requirements across dependent stages, and produce coordinated deliverables. Existing evaluations examine specific capabilities and execution settings, leaving end-to-end commission completion less understood. We introduce Visual Commission Bench (VCB), comprising 600 tasks across 12 categories and three complementary tiers, from capability-focused tasks to complete commissions. VCB uses 5,039 requirement checks and separate visual quality ratings to assess content correctness, visual realization, constraint preservation, and delivery completeness without prescribing an internal workflow. We present V-Protocol, a reference agent that dynamically composes reusable task, cognitive, and expression modules at inference time. Task modules organize delivery, cognitive modules derive content, and expression modules guide visual realization. The modules exchange structured intermediate artifacts, while a shared execution harness tracks artifact revisions and dependencies, manages tool execution, and checks completion. With the same controller and image generator as the agent baselines, V-Protocol achieves 69.0\% strict task success on VCB, compared with 42.0\% for SCOPE. On Mind-Bench, strict accuracy increases from 39.2\% to 45.4\%.
evidence_items.title: Can Image Agents Complete Visual Commissions? A Benchmark and Modular Framework

evidence_items.summary: This dataset supports the research article entitled "Effects of organic amendments on CO₂ and N₂O emissions, nutrient dynamics and biological activity in two olive-grove soils: an incubation study". The dataset contains replicate-level experimental observations and derived statistical results from a 24-day laboratory incubation conducted at 25 °C using two Mediterranean olive-grove soils from Pegalajar and Realejo (Jaén, southern Spain). Seven treatments were evaluated in triplicate: five organic amendments (cover crop residues, pruning residues, biochar, composted olive pomace and goat manure), urea as a mineral nitrogen reference, and an unamended control. The dataset includes CO₂ and N₂O emission rates and cumulative emissions, control-corrected N₂O–N release relative to applied nitrogen, pulse-derived emission metrics, mineral nitrogen concentrations (NH₄⁺–N and NO₃⁻–N), water-extractable phosphorus, soil pH, electrical conductivity, enzyme activities and microbial biomass nitrogen. Initial soil physicochemical properties, amendment composition, application rates and derived statistical analyses are also provided. Data are supplied in Excel and CSV formats, accompanied by a data dictionary, methodological documentation, quality-control information and R/Python scripts supporting the reproducibility of the analyses. The dataset is intended to facilitate transparency, verification and further research on short-term soil biogeochemical responses to organic amendments in Mediterranean olive-growing systems.
evidence_items.title: Dataset supporting the study: Effects of organic amendments on CO₂ and N₂O emissions, nutrient dynamics and biological activity in two olive-grove soils: an incubation study

evidence_items.summary: Original figures for the publication: "From Coffee Waste to Bioactive Hydrogels: In Situ Antioxidant Functionalization of Bacterial Cellulose During Biosynthesis" Abstract: Bacterial cellulose (BC) is a highly biocompatible nanofibrillar hydrogel widely explored for wound healing and tissue engineering; however, its intrinsic lack of bioactivity limits its use in advanced regenerative applications. Here, we report a one-step biosynthetic strategy that employs spent coffee grounds (SCG) extract as a dual-function cultivation medium enabling simultaneous BC production and in situ biofunctionalization. The SCG extract fully replaced glucose in Hestrin–Schramm medium, providing fermentable sugars together with naturally occurring bioactive compounds that support cellulose biosynthesis by Komagataeibacter xylinus without growth inhibition. The resulting SCG-modified BC (SCG-BC) maintained a continuous nanofibrillar network while exhibiting altered supramolecular organization, including changes in molecular weight, swelling behaviour, and hydrogel mechanics. Importantly, SCG-BC displayed strong and sustained antioxidant activity (200.23 ± 59.14 mg TE g⁻¹), indicating stable incorporation of redox-active SCG-derived constituents and limited leaching under aqueous conditions. Biological evaluation demonstrated enhanced metabolic activity of human Wharton’s jelly-derived mesenchymal stromal cells and dermal fibroblasts on SCG-BC compared to native BC, while maintaining high cell viability and adhesion. In vivo-like assessment using the quail chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) model revealed a modulated angiogenic response characterized by altered vessel density and branching without suppression of overall vascular development.
evidence_items.title: Dataset for the publication: "From Coffee Waste to Bioactive Hydrogels: In Situ Antioxidant Functionalization of Bacterial Cellulose During Biosynthesis"

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents following the ReAct paradigm are promising enablers of complex multi-step tasks, including multi-hop question answering, code generation, and control of physical AI systems. Yet, when deployed at the edge, they must tightly manage their reasoning budget while remaining reliable and deferring to a cloud-side model only when local uncertainty is too high to act safely. We propose Think Short, Defer Smart (TSDS), a framework that synergistically integrates a lightweight convergence probe, which halts on-device reasoning once the intended action has stabilized, with a perplexity-based deferral rule that escalates uncertain actions to a cloud-side model. Both mechanisms are jointly calibrated on end-to-end episode trajectories via a multi-objective Learn-Then-Test (LTT) procedure, providing simultaneous finite-sample guarantees on expected episode reward and cloud-call rate. We evaluate TSDS on four ReAct benchmarks spanning arithmetic reasoning (GSM8K), multi-hop question answering (HotpotQA), code generation (MBPP), and multi-step embodied planning (household robot), and compare against thought-calibration-only and calibrated-deferral-only standalone baselines. TSDS reduces per-episode thinking compute by 43%-65% over deferral-only baselines across HotpotQA, MBPP, and the household robot task, while maintaining certified reward and cloud-call rate guarantees.
evidence_items.title: Think Short, Defer Smart, Act, and Repeat: Calibrated Reasoning and Uncertainty-Aware Deferral for Edge LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Monitoring LLM safety at scale requires balancing cost and accuracy: a cheap latent-space probe can screen every input, but hard cases should be escalated to a more expensive expert. Existing cascades delegate based on probe uncertainty, but uncertainty is a poor proxy for the utility of an expert call, as it ignores whether the expert would actually improve the prediction. To address this problem, we introduce Calibrate-Then-Delegate (CTD), a model-cascade approach that provides probabilistic guarantees on either computation cost or safety performance while enabling instance-level (streaming) decisions. CTD builds on a novel delegation value (DV) probe, a lightweight model operating on the same internal representations as the safety probe that predicts the benefit of replacing the probe score with the expert score after an expert call. CTD calibrates a threshold on the DV signal using held-out data and multiple hypothesis testing, yielding finite-sample guarantees while optimising the complementary objective. Evaluated on four safety datasets using learned-attention probes, CTD improves over uncertainty-based delegation over much of the budget range, avoids unnecessary expert calls, and extracts positive-value subsets even from groups where the expert score is worse than the probe score on average. Ablations across four probe architectures show that these findings are not specific to any particular architecture.
evidence_items.title: Calibrate-Then-Delegate: Safety Monitoring with Risk and Budget Guarantees via Model Cascades

evidence_items.summary: Formal model evaluation methods typically certify that a model satisfies a prescribed target key performance indicator (KPI) level. However, in many applications, the relevant target KPI level may not be known a priori, and the user may instead wish to compare candidate models by analyzing the full trade-offs between performance and reliability achievable at test time by the models. This task, requiring the reliable estimate of the test-time KPI distributions, is made more complicated by the fact that the same data must often be used both to pre-select a subset of candidate models and to estimate their KPI distributions, causing a potential post-selection bias. In this work, we introduce post-selection distributional model evaluation (PS-DME), a general framework for statistically valid distributional model assessment after arbitrary data-dependent model pre-selection. Building on e-values, PS-DME controls post-selection false coverage rate (FCR) for the distributional KPI estimates and we establish explicit conditions under which it is provably more sample efficient than a baseline method based on sample splitting. Experiments on synthetic data, text-to-SQL decoding with large language models, and telecom network performance evaluation demonstrate that PS-DME enables reliable comparison of candidate configurations across a range of reliability levels, supporting the statistically reliable exploration of performance--reliability trade-offs.
evidence_items.title: Post-Selection Distributional Model Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by patients and caregivers to find health information. However, their performance in providing Simplified Chinese education on pediatric pectus excavatum (PE) remains uncertain. This study comprehensively evaluated the responses generated by five mainstream LLMs. Methods Thirty PE-related frequently asked questions (FAQs) spanning five clinical domains were collected and submitted in Simplified Chinese to ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi. Responses were evaluated by pediatric thoracic surgeons from three institutions for accuracy, completeness, and relevance, using a 6-point Likert scale. Readability was assessed using AlphaReadabilityChinese (ARC) 2.0 and the Chinese Readability Index Explorer (CRIE) 3.0. Understandability, actionability, and overall quality were evaluated with the Chinese Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (C-PEMAT-P) and the Global Quality Score (GQS). Friedman tests compared the models, followed by Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results All models achieved mean accuracy, completeness, and relevance scores above 4.9 on the 6-point scale, but the leading model differed by dimension. Claude had the highest mean accuracy (5.39 ± 0.28), completeness (5.22 ± 0.22), and GQS (4.80 ± 0.41), while DeepSeek had the highest relevance (5.42 ± 0.27). Qwen was the least readable: its median CRIE grade was 7.0, compared with 5.5 to 6.0 for the other models. Only 23.3% of its responses were at Grades 1–6, compared with 66.7–86.7% for the others. Overall C-PEMAT-P scores also differed ( p = 0.003), with Kimi showing the highest numerical mean total (12.17 ± 0.75). Qwen combined the highest actionability (2.57 ± 0.50) with the lowest understandability (9.47 ± 0.57) and GQS (3.10 ± 0.71).
evidence_items.title: Comprehensive evaluation of large language models for pediatric pectus excavatum education

evidence_items.summary: Radon measurements of the air in the soil in a 40 m deep borehole were combined with meteorological data and evaluated using artificial intelligence. The purpose of the study is to analyze the factors influencing radon levels. Neural networks were employed for this purpose. After training the neural networks, a high coefficient of determination was achieved both in the training and in the forecast (test) phase if weekly or monthly averages are used. The most influential parameters on radon content were identified using a correlation matrix. The main reasons for the large variation in radon values observed in laboratory experiments without meteorological influences were primarily the environmental conditions of decay such as water/air and the grain size or decomposition degree of the rock. When recalculating and predicting radon values, these factors must be taken into account. Otherwise the large deviations cannot be explained.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Radon Content in Soil Using Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Recent claims that large language models pass the Turing test span different procedures, but share a common focus on human outputs, rather than the processes that lead to those outputs. Here we challenge the inference from successful imitation to intelligence. Similar outputs can arise from different processes and conceal differences in reasoning, generalization, and adaptation. More fundamentally, we question whether human likeness should guide AI development at all. Prioritizing imitation can reproduce human biases, facilitate manipulation, and favor replacing people over augmenting their capabilities. AI systems should expand human welfare, not merely impersonate us. We recommend three coordinated changes: designing systems that strengthen human capabilities and independent judgment; requiring funded projects to assess benefits, costs, and their distribution; and guiding institutional procurement and renewal by evidence of AI’s effects on human welfare.
evidence_items.title: Human likeness is a misplaced benchmark for artificial intelligence

evidence_items.summary: This study evaluated four widely used large language models—ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek—as patient-information tools for e-Nabız, the national personal health record system of Türkiye, and tested whether their answers were reproducible one week apart. Thirty authentic patient questions spanning seven e-Nabız domains were submitted to each model in Turkish and English, in fresh sessions with default settings, and the protocol was repeated after one week (480 responses). A dated copy of the official e-Nabız User Guide served as the gold standard, and responses were scored blind for accuracy, completeness, the Global Quality Score, coverage, and safety, with readability computed using the Flesch, Flesch–Kincaid, Ateşman, and Bezirci–Yılmaz formulas. Model performance differed significantly in both languages, with Claude and Gemini outperforming ChatGPT and DeepSeek; two models performed better in Turkish. All models wrote above recommended reading levels, and although aggregate quality was stable between rounds, individual answers were substantially reworded and sometimes materially changed. Chatbots should complement, not replace, official e-Nabız guidance.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Patient Information Tools: A Bilingual, Two-Round Evaluation of the e-Nabız Personal Health Record System

organizations: Faculty of Engineering, Civil and Infrastructure Engineering Department, Al-Zaytoonah University of Jordan, Amman, Jordan
evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Leakage detection in water distribution networks is a critical challenge for water utilities worldwide, with deep learning (DL) emerging as a promising solution. However, the literature lacks standardized benchmarking frameworks, making it difficult to compare claims across studies and assess real-world deployability. This study presents a hybrid systematic review + experimental benchmarking approach to address this gap. A preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA)–guided systematic review of 244 records (2015–2026) from 10 engineering databases identified 71 pure DL studies. The review revealed that convolutional neural network (CNN)-based architectures were most common (35.2%), followed by autoencoders (16.9%) and long short-term memory (LSTM)/recurrent neural network architectures (12.7%). Critical gaps included reliance on simulated data (75%), lack of code or data sharing (59%), and limited reporting of computational metrics, with only 11.3% reporting inference time. The time-transformer (M5) achieved the highest detection accuracy (96.1%) and (AUC) Area Under the Curve-ROC (0.94), but required substantial computational resources. The (GGNN) Gated Graph Neural Network (M4) achieved the highest leak localization success (88.5% within 300 meters). The One-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN) deep autoencoder (M2) offered the best practical trade-off: fast inference (3.5 ms), strong noise robustness (9.9% drop at 20 dB signal-to-noise ratio), unsupervised training, and 92.6% accuracy. The lightweight 1D-CNN (M3) was most efficient (12 MB, 1.2 hours) but degraded by 14.5% under noise. The LSTM-autoencoder (M1) achieved 91.3% accuracy and 86.1% recall.
evidence_items.title: Deep learning for leakage detection in water distribution networks: a systematic review and benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Astrological consultations can create anxiety when adverse predictions are communicated through direct or fatalistic language particularly in culturally subjective contexts where users may attach personal meaning to such predictions. This empirical study investigates whether empathetic AI mediated communication can influence user trust, anxiety and emotional relief when compared with conventional blunt communication by human practitioners. The study introduces two complementary contributions. An AI based semantic reframing approach and an emotional Human Computer Interaction interface framework. The AI approach uses a safety constrained large language model to identify catastrophic or deterministic elements in astrological narratives and transform them into constructive, non-deterministic and growth-oriented interpretations. The HCI framework examines how conversational language, reduced textual density, supportive formatting, and non-deterministic interface structures can contribute to a more emotionally supportive user experience while preserving user agency. A multi demographic user survey was conducted in which participants evaluated identical stressful astrological scenarios presented through a traditional blunt human practitioner script and a safety constrained AI generated narrative. Participants assessed perceived trust, anxiety, emotional relief and overall experience across the two conditions. The findings indicate that human practitioner communication retained a perception of authenticity whereas the AI mediated condition was associated with lower reported anxiety and greater emotional relief. The combination of empathetic linguistic reframing and supportive HCI presentation also showed a positive relationship with experiential trust and perceived user agency. These findings suggest that the emotional impact of AI-mediated communication depends not only on the content generated but also on how that content is structured and presented to users. The study contributes to research on empathetic AI, emotional HCI and responsible conversational design by demonstrating how safety constrained language generation and supportive interface design can facilitate less deterministic, emotionally supportive and user centered experiences in culturally sensitive domains. The findings provide a foundation for further investigation of responsible AI communication in emotionally subjective digital environments.
evidence_items.title: The Comforting Machine: Evaluating User Trust and Emotional Relief in Empathetic AI Astrologers vs Blunt Human Practitioners

evidence_items.summary:
The increased use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) detection systems in higher education has led to new challenges for both undergraduates and academics. However, existing research is primarily normative and future-oriented and has largely focused on evaluating the reliability of AI detectors or proposing future policy reforms. Accordingly, limited attention has been given to students’ and academics’ lived experiences, particularly the compounded pressure they face when writing simultaneously to bypass AI detection systems and satisfy subsequent human evaluators in online assignment submissions. Additionally, English as a Second Language (ESL) undergraduates’ lived experiences in navigating such difficulties remain underexplored. Therefore, this study investigates the linguistic strategies employed by computing undergraduates when writing simultaneously for AI detection systems and human evaluators in online assignment submissions, and the academic writing teaching methods currently adopted by academics to help students manage the pressure of producing both algorithmically acceptable and academically acceptable writing. The study employed a qualitative multi-method design involving 30 computing undergraduates from three higher education institutes in Sri Lanka and seven lecturers teaching Academic English to computing students. Data were collected through focus group discussions with undergraduates, semi-structured interviews with academics, and textual analysis of selected
student assignments. Thematic analysis was used to analyse the data. The study found that undergraduates adopt multi-layered linguistic strategies to reduce probabilistic regularity in AI-generated writing patterns, including sentence variation, lexical diversification, conversational markers, and rhetorical questioning to improve perceived authenticity. Additionally, interviews with academics revealed varied and conflicting responses, ranging from complete acceptance of AI integration to its strict rejection, including teaching paraphrasing, academic integrity, citation, AI literacy instruction, process-based writing instruction, development of authorial voice, reflective tasks, and vivas based on online assignment submissions. It can be concluded that AI detection demands have exacerbated the academic writing difficulties of ESL learners, transforming academic writing into a dual-audience challenge. Theoretically, the study contributes to emerging literature on AI in education by examining ESL undergraduates’ linguistic practices. Practically, the findings highlight the need for consistent pedagogical approaches to AI use in academic writing, and the need for clearer and more transparent institutional AI policies.
evidence_items.title: Writing for Two Judges: Computing Undergraduates’ Linguistic Strategies for Navigating Artificial Intelligence Detection Systems and Human Evaluation in Online Assignment Writing

evidence_items.summary:
Objectives:
 This study examined dental hygiene students' perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted instruction and the factors influencing their satisfaction with such classes.
 Methods:
 A self-administered questionnaire was completed by 80 dental hygiene students who participated in an AI-assisted course. The survey evaluated AI usability, the perceived usefulness of learning activities, learning outcomes, and overall class satisfaction. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, independent t-tests, and a hierarchical multiple regression analysis.
 Results:
 The mean scores for AI usability and perceived usefulness for learning activities were 4.30 and 4.23, respectively. Among the learning outcomes, collaborative competency received the highest mean score of 4.08, followed by academic achievement at 3.91 and learning motivation and self-efficacy at 3.85. The mean class satisfaction score was 3.76. Students who demonstrated higher AI competency, academic achievement, expected course grades, teamwork, and learning participation reported significantly greater AI usability, perceived usefulness of learning activities, learning outcomes, and class satisfaction (p<0.001). The results of the regression analysis showed that learning outcomes (β=0.381, p<0.001) were the most influential factor on class satisfaction, and academic achievement (β=0.289, p<0.001) and AI competency (β=0.193, p=0.013) were also identified as related factors.
 Conclusions:
 These findings indicate that dental hygiene students hold positive perceptions of AI-assisted classes. Importantly, learning outcomes emerge as critical determinants of class satisfaction. Therefore, AI-assisted education should extend beyond the mere introduction of AI tools by enhancing AI literacy and integrating AI thoughtfully into instructional design.
evidence_items.title: Dental hygiene students' perceptions of artificial intelligence-assisted classes and factors associated with class satisfaction

evidence_items.summary: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence, industrial Internet of Things and smart manufacturing technologies is improving production efficiency and operational intelligence while changing how workers interact and communicate with intelligent systems. However, existing automation approaches often prioritize productivity and process optimization with less attention to workforce sustainability, human involvement and long-term human AI collaboration. This research proposes a human centered AI automation framework for sustainable smart manufacturing within the Industry 5.0 paradigm, with particular attention to human AI communication, digital interaction and collaborative decision making. The framework integrates AI, IoT, predictive analytics, computer vision and real time decision support to support human capabilities rather than replace workers. Production, machine and workforce related data will be considered to support resource utilization, identify potential operational disruptions, balance workloads and assist human decision making. The framework will be evaluated using technical performance measures and workforce related assessments. A Human AI Collaboration Index will be developed to assess workforce acceptance, trust, communication effectiveness, collaboration quality and sustainable productivity, providing a structured measure of human AI collaboration. A mixed method approach will be employed, combining quantitative operational and production performance measures with qualitative assessments of workforce interaction, communication, trust and acceptance. Quantitative data will be analyzed using appropriate descriptive and inferential statistical procedures while qualitative data will be examined through thematic analysis to identify patterns related to human AI interaction and workforce sustainability. Framework validation will be conducted in two stages, component level testing of the proposed AI and decision support functions followed by integrated evaluation against predefined technical, communication and human centered criteria. The expected outcomes are evidence regarding the potential of the framework to support production intelligence, efficient resource utilization, workforce engagement, operational resilience and sustainable human AI collaboration. Rather than assuming these benefits before empirical validation, the study will examine their potential through the proposed evaluation process. The research contributes to Industry 5.0 by connecting AI enabled manufacturing with human AI communication and digital interaction while providing a human centered approach for evaluating collaborative automation and workforce sustainability.
evidence_items.title: Human Centered AI Automation Framework for Sustainable Smart Manufacturing: Enhancing Production Intelligence While Preserving Workforce Sustainability in Industry 5.0

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence has introduced new visual possibilities, generated an immense number of images and photographs each day, often without clear authorship or ownership. Dance, as a cultural form, represents the traditions of a country and plays a significant role in shaping society both aesthetically and as a form of entertainment. Dance photography is particularly important, as it preserves cultural authenticity and serves as a visual record for future generations. However, while AI-generated images offer new ways of representing cultural heritage, they also raise critical concerns regarding authenticity, ownership, and cultural responsibility. This study examines the cultural effectiveness and traditional authenticity of AI-generated dance imagery featured in the People’s Bank Calendar 2025 of Sri Lanka. Adopting a mixed-methods approach, the research integrates visual content analysis, audience evaluation, and expert insights to assess how these images represent the essence of Sri Lankan traditional dance forms. The visual analysis focuses on identifying key traditional elements such as costume, gestures, and symbolic motifs. A structured questionnaire is administered to a purposive sample of 20 respondents with prior knowledge or experience in traditional dance, in order to obtain informed evaluations of authenticity, aesthetic quality, and cultural appropriateness. In addition, semi-structured interviews with dance practitioners and cultural experts provide deeper insights into the accuracy and implications of AI-mediated cultural representation. Quantitative data are analyzed using descriptive statistics, qualitative findings are analyzed using thematic analysis. The study aims to examine how artificial intelligence interacts with traditional and cultural forms through the generation of dance imagery and photographs, and how these representations influence audience perceptions. It further seeks to evaluate whether AI-generated visuals can preserve and effectively communicate intangible cultural heritage without compromising its traditional integrity.
evidence_items.title: Digital Steps, Traditional Roots: Evaluating Cultural Authenticity and Audience Response to AI-Generated Dance Imagery in the People’s Bank Calendar 2025

evidence_items.summary: Depression is a major global mental health concern and the increasing use of artificial intelligence in digital interventions has created opportunities for more adaptive and user centered approaches to prevention and early intervention. However, existing digital mental health solutions continue to face limitations such as static personalization, limited emotion recognition, single modal interaction, accessibility constraints, limited adaptability and ethical and user experience concerns. This study proposes a multi framework AI powered UX approach to explore how these limitations can be addressed through adaptive, multimodal, accessible, immersive and ethically informed technologies. The proposed approach consists of six complementary frameworks of which five are implemented as independent technological simulations and one Ethical UX Integration is developed conceptually. The Adaptive UX framework demonstrates emotion-based interface adaptation while the Voice User Interface framework explores emotion aware voice interaction. The Accessibility framework demonstrates adaptive interface complexity based on user interaction ability and the AR/VR Gamification framework explores immersive and emotionally responsive relaxation experiences. The Multimodal AR Support framework demonstrates personalized responses through the combination of multiple input modalities. These frameworks are designed to operate independently while supporting a conceptual integration through a common decision oriented approach. The study is guided by user-specific factors including personalization, emotional sensitivity, interaction preference, accessibility, engagement and cognitive comfort. A proof-of-concept evaluation using pre and post intervention questionnaires is conducted to examine perceived changes in user experience and emotional responses. The simulations demonstrate the technical feasibility of applying adaptive personalization, emotion aware interaction, accessibility adaptation, immersive engagement and multimodal support within depression related digital UX contexts. The evaluation provides preliminary evidence of perceived changes in engagement, comfort, personalization and interaction experience. However, these findings do not represent clinical evidence of depression treatment effectiveness. The study therefore contributes a technically and conceptually grounded approach that connects AI, UX, accessibility, multimodal interaction, immersive technologies and ethical considerations while providing a basis for future empirical validation and extension to other domains requiring adaptive and user centered human computer interaction.
evidence_items.title: Design of a Multi-Framework AI-Powered UX System for Ethical and Immersive Depression Intervention

evidence_items.summary: Background: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory condition associated with periodontal pathogens, and conventional systemic antimicrobial therapy may be associated with systemic adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance. Localized delivery of antimicrobial agents directly into periodontal pockets may improve drug retention at the site of infection while reducing unnecessary systemic exposure. Metronidazole is particularly useful against anaerobic microorganisms associated with periodontal infections. The present study aimed to develop and evaluate a metronidazole-loaded mucoadhesive emulgel for localized periodontal drug delivery. Methods: Metronidazole emulgels were prepared using Carbopol 940 and Carbopol 934 as gelling agents. The formulation consisted of an oil-in-water emulsion incorporated into a gel base containing liquid paraffin, Span 20, Tween 20, propylene glycol, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, and other suitable excipients. Six formulations (F1–F6) were prepared using different concentrations of Carbopol 940 or Carbopol 934. The prepared formulations were evaluated for physical appearance, homogeneity, pH, viscosity, spreadability, extrudability, drug content, and grittiness. Results: All formulations exhibited satisfactory physical characteristics and were free from phase separation and grittiness. The formulations showed variations in viscosity with changes in polymer concentration, with higher Carbopol concentrations producing greater viscosity. Spreadability was inversely related to viscosity. Drug content ranged from 95.0% to 97.2%, with F3 showing the highest value (97.2%) and F6 showing 97.0%. The evaluated formulations demonstrated acceptable extrusion characteristics, with F1, F3, and F6 reported as having excellent extrudability. Conclusion: The developed metronidazole emulgel formulations demonstrated satisfactory physicochemical properties and drug content, indicating their potential as localized periodontal drug delivery systems. Among the prepared formulations, F1, F3, and F6 were identified in the manuscript as promising formulations based on their overall physicochemical characteristics. However, further studies involving in-vitro drug release, mucoadhesive strength, periodontal retention, microbiological efficacy, comprehensive stability testing, and in-vivo evaluation are required before establishing therapeutic effectiveness.
evidence_items.title: Formulation Optimization and Evaluation of Metronidazole Emulgel for Localized Management of Periodontal Infections

evidence_items.summary:
Inflammation is a natural physiological process involved in many acute and chronic diseases and there is a great need
for developing new safer, natural anti-inflammatory agents․ Chitosan is a biocompatible polysaccharide, produced by
chitin deacetylation, and has been extensively studied due to its several biological activities, including anti-inflammatory
properties․ The in vitro anti-inflammatory effect of commercial chitosan was compared with that of fish chitosan sourced
from two species: Labeo rohita, and Anabas testudineus․ The modes of action of the anti-inflammatory activity of the
chitosan were determined by measuring its ability to inhibit proteinase and hyaluronidase, as well as its Lipoxygenase
(LOX) inhibition activity (assessed by LOX reaction with a synthetic substrate) and its membrane stabilising activity
(determined by the polysaccharide’s ability to reduce heat-induced and hypotonicity-induced hemolysis)․ In this
study, anti-inflammatory drugs such as diclofenac sodium, aspirin and indomethacin were used as positive control․ A
concentration-dependent inhibition of inflammation-related processes was found in all chitosan samples․ For commercial
chitosan, greater inhibition was achieved at a lower concentration, whereas fish chitosan had the same or greater inhibition
at a higher concentration․ The in vitro anti-inflammatory potential of the fish-based extracts was attributed to L. rohita and
A. testudineus chitosan based on enzyme inhibition and membrane stabilisation measurements․ The proteinase inhibitory
activity increased dose-dependently, with commercial chitosan showing the highest inhibition among the fish-derived
chitosans (59.75% at 500 μg/mL), followed by L. rohita (40.25%) and A. testudineus,/i> (32.94%), as compare to positive
control. The anti-inflammatory activity of chitosan is likely caused by a combination of the inhibition of inflammation-related
enzymes and the stabilisation of cellular membranes against inflammatory damage․This study suggests that the
source and concentration of chitosan influence its biological activities, and that chitosan from fish, especially L. rohita, has
noteworthy anti-inflammatory properties with the potential to act as a promising alternative to commercial chitosan․ The
valorisation of fish-processing waste as a sustainable source of bioactive chitosan could provide a substrate for subsequent
in vivo studies and set the stage for clinical trials on new anti-inflammatory drugs․
Major Findings: This study suggests that the source and concentration of chitosan influence its biological activities,
and that chitosan from fish, especially L. rohita, has noteworthy anti-inflammatory activity with the potential to act as a
promising alternative to commercial chitosan․
evidence_items.title: Comparative Evaluation of Anti-Inflammatory Properties of Chitosan Extracted from the Scales of Labeo rohita and Anabas testudineus: An In Vitro Study

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Emotional Reappraisal (MER) aims to shift affective interpretation by rewriting and editing a situation without altering its underlying semantic context. Despite advances in controllable editing and sentiment transfer, MER remains challenging under coupled multimodal constraints, especially in internet memes where images, embedded text, and layout jointly encode affective meaning. To bridge this gap, we present MER-Bench, a systematic benchmark for MER on image-text memes, containing over 3,000 real-world memes with fine-grained annotations for emotion transformation and structure-preserving multimodal editing. MER-Bench spans diverse visual, textual, and structural settings and is paired with a structured MLLM-as-a-Judge evaluation suite, comprising eight fine-grained metrics and three aggregated objectives for emotional alignment, content fidelity, and transformation strength. Extensive evaluation of 14 advanced multimodal models reveals that: (1) current models struggle to jointly balance affect, semantics, structure, and text; (2) strong visual editing does not imply effective MER, with poor embedded text rendering and affect-aware rewriting remaining key bottlenecks. Our results identify MER as a critical capability gap in current multimodal generation systems and highlight affective image-text reasoning as a key challenge for future work. Project Page: https://github.com/one-seven17/MER-Bench
evidence_items.title: MER-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Emotional Reappraisal for Image-Text Memes

evidence_items.summary: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
evidence_items.title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how prompt design influences the quality of large language model (LLM)-generated business-to-business (B2B) market research outputs. It also proposes a switch-point governance mechanism for converting LLM-generated drafts into decision-ready market intelligence artefacts. Design/methodology/approach The study uses an exploratory pilot evaluation of three market-facing LLM-based tools: ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity AI. The tools are compared across three benchmark B2B market research tasks and three prompt types: basic, context-augmented and role-specific. In total, 81 outputs were generated. A role-specific benchmark subset of 27 outputs was then assessed using automated metrics and blinded human ratings. The automated metrics included relevance through cosine similarity, reference overlap through ROUGE-F1, cross-run semantic stability, latency, token length and readability through Flesch Reading Ease. Human evaluators rated the outputs on relevance, completeness, factuality, instruction-following and insightfulness. One-way ANOVA and non-parametric checks are reported as exploratory task-level tests, not as confirmatory evidence of model superiority. Findings Role-specific prompts produced the strongest descriptive scores in this pilot setting. Within the benchmark subset, Gemini showed the strongest observed profile, with higher average relevance, reference overlap and semantic stability, along with lower latency. ChatGPT produced relevant outputs but tended to generate longer and less readable drafts. Perplexity generated concise and readable summaries, but its outputs were less aligned with the reference brief and decision-facing requirements. Human ratings followed a similar descriptive pattern. Cross-run semantic stability showed directional alignment with higher decision-readiness ratings, offering preliminary support for P1.
evidence_items.title: Advancing value creation in B2B market research – a human–AI collaboration framework for large language model

evidence_items.summary: Large language models often deviate from the target word count when following length constraints such as “generate X words.” Existing studies mostly focus on content quality, while paying relatively less attention to format control, especially the accuracy of length control. To address this issue, this study builds a Chinese text generation benchmark covering 5 topics and 4 word-count levels, and evaluates three representative models: DeepSeek-V3, Tongyi Qianwen (Qwen2.5), and Kimi. Based on this, a lightweight post-processing framework, LAPP (Length-Aware Post-Processing), is proposed. When the output is too long, LAPP uses sentence-level intelligent truncation; when the output is too short, it calls Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct for semantics-preserving expansion, and controls the length error within ±10% through iterative correction. The experimental results show that the original average deviation rates of the three models are 11.93%–38.70%, which are reduced to about 5% after LAPP correction, and the pass rate increases from 20%–70% to 85%–100%. The semantic preservation results show an average BERTScore of 0.97 between the corrected and original texts, suggesting that the framework improves length control while largely keeping the original meaning. This study shows that the “rough generation + precise correction” approach is effective for word-count control, and offers a low-cost, transferable way to improve the instruction-following ability of large language models.
evidence_items.title: Research on the Length Controllability of Chinese Large Language Model Outputs Based on Post-Processing Correction

evidence_items.summary: Abstract User reviews of mobile applications provide a source of citizen feedback on digital public services, yet their automated analysis in non-English settings is constrained by the limited availability of domain-adapted classifiers. This study develops and evaluates a documented procedure for three-class sentiment classification of Czech reviews of government mobile applications using a large language model without task-specific fine-tuning. The corpus comprised 10,198 reviews of six applications. An adjudicated human reference was created for a stratified random sample of 500 reviews, and LLM performance was compared with a majority-class baseline, two lexicon-based methods, and two readily deployable encoder-based transfer models. The validation included five repeated runs under identical settings and an analysis of classification errors. Across five GPT-5.6 Sol validation runs, mean accuracy was 93.0%, mean macro-F1 was 0.827, and mean Cohen's kappa was 0.857. Macro-F1 ranged from 0.814 to 0.845, while agreement among the five runs was high (Fleiss' kappa = 0.918). The neutral class was the most challenging, with most disagreements occurring at its boundaries with negative and positive sentiment. In the full corpus, 65.9% of reviews were classified as negative, 7.9% as neutral, and 26.2% as positive. Textual sentiment was strongly associated with star ratings but was not identical to them. These findings provide corpus-specific evidence that a standardized LLM procedure can help analyze short-form non-english citizen feedback. They also underscore the need for human reference labels, stability checks, and precise documentation of the model, prompt, settings, and execution workflow.
evidence_items.title: Sentiment Analysis of Government Mobile App Reviews: Validating Zero-Shot Classification with a Large Language Model
