evidence_items.summary: Phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS) is the practical state of the art for large arrays of optical traps, but it optimizes the hologram on an ideal model of the spatial light modulator (SLM), and the sequences that move traps interpolate between holograms that were never optimized for the frames in between. We test two hypotheses against the strongest baselines on the same scalar Fourier model. First, keeping the WGS weights but replacing the phase update by conjugate-gradient steps through the pixel-crosstalk kernel and the phase quantizer of the device (device-aware WGS) lowers the trap-intensity spread on the device. On a 10 x 10 lattice behind a crosstalk device, the relative standard deviation falls from a median of 5.21 percent for phase-fixed WGS at 30 iterations (5.21 percent at 100) to 0.205 percent, a median factor of 26 over 5 seeds (range 16 to 33) at a median 0.995 of the baseline's efficiency; the factor is 7.9 with 4-bit phase and a fill factor of 0.85 added, and 2.0 on a smaller 8 x 8 grid with flicker added and a fixed 30-iteration budget (the ratio of the means of 3 seeds); over the 5 geometries of the studio's benchmark on that device the median factor is 1.73 (0.97 to 4.69), and 2 of them meet both thresholds. A control that removes the device model from the loop gains nothing (5.14 percent), so the gain comes from the model. Second, optimizing every intermediate hologram of a moving-trap sequence with the trap phases locked to a smooth trajectory (flicker-bounded sequence) keeps the minimum transient intensity of the moving traps at a median 0.920 of their mean (range 0.915 to 0.932) over 5 seeds at 13 frames (below 0.9 at seven frames), against 0.654 (0.551 to 0.709) for linear phase interpolation.
evidence_items.title: Device-Aware Weighted Gerchberg-Saxton and Flicker-Bounded Phase-Continuous Sequences for Holographic Optical Trap Arrays

evidence_items.summary: This study aimed to determine teachers’ competency in designing AI- This study determined the relationship between teachers’ classroom accommodation practices and their use of emerging digital tools among teachers of Matab-ang National High School, Division of Toledo City, during School Year 2026–2027. It specifically described the respondents’ demographic profile, determined the levels of classroom accommodation practices and use of emerging digital tools, and established whether a significant relationship existed between the variables. A descriptive-correlational research design was employed in Matab-ang National High School. Fifty teacher-respondents were selected through purposive sampling. An adapted and contextualized survey questionnaire covering demographic profile, classroom accommodation practices, and use of emerging digital tools served as the instrument. Frequency and percentage, weighted mean, standard deviation, and Pearson Product-Moment Correlation Coefficient were used to analyze the data. Results showed that teachers demonstrated strong classroom accommodation practices and regular use of emerging digital tools. However, differentiated learning activities, assessment methods, online collaboration, exploration of newly introduced technologies, and digital applications for differentiated instruction were less consistently practiced. A significant positive relationship existed between classroom accommodation practices and use of emerging digital tools. The study concluded that purposeful use of emerging digital tools was associated with stronger classroom accommodation practices. An Action Plan was recommended to strengthen differentiated instruction, flexible assessment, online collaboration, and technology integration through targeted training, hands-on activities, peer sharing, and classroom-based application, and continuous monitoring and evaluation for sustained improvement.
evidence_items.title: Teachers' Classroom Accommodation Practices and Teachers' Use of Emerging Digital Tools

evidence_items.summary: This is the Replication package for the paper  “Pattern Hunters: Agents for Microservice API Pattern Detection.” We investigated whether LLM-based coding agents can automatically detect  Microservice API Patterns (MAPs)  in open-source microservice systems. Starting from three published datasets, we selected  100 open-source microservice repositories  and built a knowledge base of the  45 MAPs  from the official pattern catalogue, together with a detection specification given to every agent as a reusable skill.  Nine agent–LLM configurations  — the coding agents Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and OpenCode, each combined with the LLMs GLM-5.2, Kimi-K2.7-Code and MiniMax-M3 served through Ollama Cloud — judged, for every repository and every pattern, whether the pattern is present. That is 4,500 repository–pattern pairs per configuration run, and the whole study was  executed three times , giving  2,700 agent runs  in total. We then measured the agreement between configurations, detection performance against 1,065 manually labelled pairs, and the consistency of the results across the three runs. This package contains everything needed to verify or extend that analysis: the repository selection trail, the knowledge base and the detection specification, the untouched output of all 2,700 agent runs, every intermediate and final result, and all analysis scripts. Licence Scripts are released under the  MIT License ; data files are released under  CC BY 4.0 . What is in the package DataCollection/  — the full selection trail from the 415 candidate projects of the three source datasets down to the 100 analysed repositories, including the language criteria and the clone URL and exact commit of every repository.
evidence_items.title: Replication Package for "Pattern Hunters: Agents for Microservice API Pattern Detection"

evidence_items.summary: A phase-only spatial light modulator in the pupil of a microscope objective can form hundreds to thousands of optical traps at once, but only if the phase pattern it displays is computed well: the pattern fixes how much light reaches the traps, how equal the traps are, where stray light goes, how the pattern survives a real device, and how fast it can be recomputed when traps move. DinHot is an open studio that runs 24 ladder methods (10 classical, 9 state of the art, 5 beyond it) on the same task, with the same seeds, metrics and device model, in Python as the reference and in a TypeScript port that runs live in a browser. We describe the optical and device model, the methods with the measured acceptance of each, 14 cases from a 3 x 3 array to a disordered 819-trap array and shaped potentials, the benchmark protocol, two learned models, and the 5 proposals past the published state of the art, three of which meet their ladder criteria on their acceptance tasks, each within a scope that the benchmark or the scope measurements narrow (a device-aware weighted Gerchberg-Saxton update, a flicker-bounded phase-continuous sequence and an efficiency-uniformity front), one of which meets a narrowed criterion (an aberration-robust hologram) and one of which is refuted by measurement (a learned warm start for phase-fixed weighted GS). A network trained on three-plane volumes beats its baseline at equal wall-clock on all 162 held-out volumes (median accuracy ratio 1.140), whereas its two-dimensional counterpart ties with Gerchberg-Saxton (ratio 0.9994). The model is a scalar Fourier model of a simulated device, not a calibrated instrument. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CEFOP DinHot . Interactive studio: https://dinhot.fasl-work.com .

evidence_items.summary: Stack Overflow’s community-driven maintenance model faces mounting pressure from declining participation following the mainstream adoption of large language models (LLMs). This study introduces the reliability-trajectory framework to address this gap, sampling 1,500 focal-answer trajectories across four language ecosystems (Python, JavaScript, Java, C#), spanning symmetric pre-LLM and post-LLM observation windows. Each trajectory was manually annotated for failure presence, type, temporal origin, detection channel, repair status, and persistence. Survival analysis, logistic regression, and a 250-case LLM benchmark complemented the annotation.  This replication package contains relevant details for the accompanying manuscript. Refer to README.md for further usage details.

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objectives To assess the feasibility of using a locally hosted large language model (LLM) to generate patient-friendly radiology reports while avoiding cloud transfer of report text. Materials and methods In this retrospective study, 360 chest, knee, lumbar spine, and shoulder X-rays, and shoulder and abdominal ultrasound reports from Dutch primary care were included. Main report sections ( n = 359) and conclusion sections ( n = 350) were translated into patient-friendly versions using Gemma-3 (12B parameters) and assessed for accuracy and completeness on 5-point Likert scales. Readability was evaluated using text length and Flesch–Douma reading ease (FDRE) scores. Hallucinations were systematically documented. Statistical analyses included Kruskal–Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and paired t tests. Results Patient-friendly conclusions achieved higher median accuracy scores than main reports (5 [Q1–Q3 5–5] vs 4 [3–5]), while completeness scores were high for both sections (5 [5–5]). Compared with original reports, patient-friendly reports were longer (median increase 65 words [48–84], p < 0.001) and had higher FDRE scores (mean increase 54.2 ± 18.8, p < 0.001). Overall, 71.0% of main reports and 96.0% of conclusions met predefined quality criteria (accuracy and completeness ≥ 4), while 48.0% of combined main report and conclusion sections met both quality and readability criteria (FDRE score > 60). Clinically relevant hallucinations occurred in 45 reports (12.5%). Conclusion A locally hosted LLM demonstrated feasibility for generating patient-friendly translations of Dutch X-ray and ultrasound reports while avoiding cloud transfer of data, with better performance for conclusion sections than main reports. However, clinically relevant hallucinations remain a safety concern and indicate the need for clinician oversight and further evaluation before clinical implementation.
evidence_items.title: Generating patient-friendly radiology reports with a local large language model: expert evaluation of quality and readability

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate fluent responses but may overlook relevant evidence or violate task and safety constraints. This survey examines MLLM alignment through two complementary gaps: the Modality Gap, concerning cross-modal correspondence and the use of task-relevant evidence, and the Intent Gap, concerning behavior relative to specified goals, constraints, and human expectations. We organize the literature along six dimensions: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. Across these dimensions, we link alignment mechanisms and supervision assumptions to the failures they target and the evidence supporting their effectiveness. Our analysis clarifies what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment, together with the limitations of their underlying supervision. We further summarize evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels, emphasizing evidence dependence, constraint compliance, and the distinction between observed improvements and explanations of their underlying mechanisms. Applications in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support reveal three recurring requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and decisions that respect domain constraints. Building on this synthesis, we identify four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, diagnosis-guided repair, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.
evidence_items.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND Patient-facing conversational artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly deployed across health care to sustain two-way patient communication and collect patient-reported data at scale. Their workflows include a classification layer that reads each free-text message and routes it to an appropriate response. Performing this triage with a large language model (LLM) is accurate but carries recurring cost and latency at scale and sends sensitive patient text to an external service; a smaller, locally hosted model is cheap, private, and controllable but is less reliable on ambiguous or out-of-scope (out-of-distribution) messages and can make clinically consequential errors. F1 metrics compound the problem by treating every error as equivalent, while in this context misclassifying a safety-critical message is far more harmful than confusing two benign categories. We evaluate triage errors using an asymmetric clinical cost matrix. OBJECTIVE We aimed to develop and retrospectively evaluate a two-stage triage system that preserves LLM-level quality while reducing how often the LLM is called. We evaluate it by clinical consequence rather than by raw error count. METHODS A compact local classifier handled routine messages, and an LLM was invoked only when accepting the local prediction carried high expected clinical cost. The routing rule is the system’s central design choice: each message is escalated by its expected clinical cost under an asymmetric, expert-elicited cost matrix, rather than by generic confidence or uncertainty. The local classifier is a fine-tuned text-embedding encoder trained with outlier exposure and a geometry-aware output head (a Semantic-Anchor Equiangular Tight Frame, SA-ETF, that aligns maximally separated class directions to each category’s clinical description).
evidence_items.title: Selective Large Language Model Support for Patient-Message Triage in Remote Care: A Cost-Aware Hybrid Approach (Preprint)

evidence_items.summary: Educational institutions face increasing pressure to adapt their curricula to the rapidly evolving demands of the job market, and recommender systems can be important tools to guide students in selecting courses that align with their career goals. We present EdFitter, a hybrid course recommendation system that combines pretrained text embeddings for retrieval with large language models (LLMs) used offline for semantic skill extraction. The system is designed for a cold-start setting in which free-text job queries must be matched to a university’s institutional course catalog. Instead of relying on direct generative recommendations, EdFitter ranks stored course descriptions by cosine similarity and augments the output with extracted skills and matching vacancy examples. We evaluate the system in a pilot institutional deployment at Higher School of Economics (HSE) using a multi-level study with student respondents, controlled assessors, and interviews with program directors. The results indicate that users perceive the recommendations as sufficiently relevant and potentially useful to justify further development. Overall, the study suggests that EdFitter is a valuable tool for supporting course exploration and curriculum-to-labor-market alignment; we also highlight important limitations and directions for future work.
evidence_items.title: EdFitter: a hybrid course recommendation system using large language models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for patient education and medical information delivery. However, their outputs may involve trade-offs among medical accuracy, comprehensiveness, empathy, and readability. Type 2 diabetes remission is a clinically nuanced concept that is readily misunderstood by patients, making it a suitable context in which to evaluate both the medical quality and patient accessibility of artificial intelligence–generated health information. To systematically compare the medical quality and readability of responses concerning type 2 diabetes remission generated by different LLMs and prompting strategies, and to characterize their joint quality–readability profiles. We conducted a cross-sectional study using a balanced factorial design. Responses were generated for 16 core questions concerning type 2 diabetes remission using 4 LLMs—DeepSeek-V3.2,GPT-5.5,Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4.6—and 6 prompting strategies: Keyword, Question, 6th-grade, Guideline, Patient, and Doctor. This yielded 384 AI-generated responses. Two endocrinologists, each with more than 5 years of clinical experience, independently evaluated medical quality using a prespecified rubric. Five domains—Accuracy, Relevance, Comprehensiveness, Empathy, and Falsehood avoidance—were rated on 5-point ordinal scales. A descriptive Composite quality score was also calculated. Readability was assessed using the Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES), Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), Gunning Fog Index (GFOG), and Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG). Quality ratings were analyzed using cumulative link mixed models, whereas readability outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models; Question ID was included as a random intercept in all models. Exploratory analyses examined Spearman correlations between readability and quality and identified Pareto-efficient model–prompt combinations.
evidence_items.title: Quality and readability of large language model–generated responses on type 2 diabetes remission: a cross-sectional balanced factorial study
Exploring the adoption and evaluation of artificial intelligence research tools in licensed electronic resources

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an exceptionally powerful tool for analyzing scientific data. In particular, attention-based architectures have demonstrated a remarkable capability to capture complex correlations and to furnish interpretable insights into latent, otherwise inconspicuous patterns. This progress motivates the application of AI techniques to the analysis of strongly correlated electrons, which remain notoriously challenging to study using conventional theoretical approaches. Here, we propose AI workflows for analyzing snapshot datasets from tensor-network simulations of the two-dimensional (2D) Hubbard model over a broad range of temperature and doping. The 2D Hubbard model is an archetypal strongly correlated system, hosting diverse intriguing phenomena including Mott insulators, anomalous metals, and high- T c superconductivity. Our AI techniques yield fresh perspectives on the intricate quantum correlations underpinning these phenomena and facilitate universal omnimetry for ultracold-atom simulations of the corresponding strongly correlated systems.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable Artificial Intelligence Analysis of Strongly Correlated Electrons

evidence_items.summary: In the context of foreign language writing, studies suggest that Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)-assisted learning supports knowledge acquisition and increases motivation (Chen & Gong, 2025). However, its use requires a meticulous implementation due to deficiencies in academic rigor and citation accuracy, as well as the risk of over-reliance (Chen & Gong, 2025; Solak, 2024). Through a quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-intervention measures, this study evaluates the efficacy of a GenAI-mediated pedagogical sequence on argumentative writing performance. Following a process-based writing approach (Flower & Hayes, 1981), 39 second-year English Language Teaching (ELT) students participated in five sessions focused on self-assessment and draft editing. These sessions were assisted by tools such as Gemin (for IELTS rubric-based draft evaluation), Quillbot (for grammar and style correction), and Lextutor (for lexical profiling). The results confirm that GenAI —when integrated into a structured sequence— seems to strengthen L2 writing clarity, making it more precise and readable by optimizing feedback and promoting the critical, self-regulated use of these tools for essay improvement. Furthermore, the high level of student satisfaction with the resources used highlights the importance of fostering digital literacy and enhancing the role of GenAI as a pedagogical complement. This approach promotes the ethical integration of emerging technologies into writing instruction within Higher Education.
evidence_items.title: Inteligencia artificial generativa y escritura autorregulada

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Marine structures such as ships and offshore platforms often suffer structural deformation during service due to factors including collision and corrosion. After deformation occurs, the rapid evaluation of the hydrodynamic performance of structures is a prerequisite for ensuring safety and formulating maintenance strategies. To this end, this paper establishes a rapid evaluation framework for the hydrodynamic performance of deformed marine structures, which integrates image acquisition, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Three-Dimensional (3D) reconstruction, numerical simulation, and emergency decision-making. The specific procedure of the framework consists of four steps: First, a multi-view image acquisition scheme for structures considering deformed regions is designed to collect two-dimensional images and complete preprocessing. Second, the 3D model of the structure is reconstructed based on the HunYuan3D model, followed by preprocessing operations such as hole filling and topological repair. Third, the processed model is imported into hydrodynamic software to complete the numerical simulation and performance evaluation of the structure. Finally, a follow-up disposal plan is formulated and decision-making suggestions are provided based on the evaluation results.The framework is validated on a deformed ship: the errors of the governing geometric parameters of the reconstructed model are within 3%, and the simulated deterioration of the stability reserve and motion responses is consistent with the mechanisms reported for damaged hulls. Positioning the framework as a rapid preliminary screening and decision-support tool for emergency scenarios, the results demonstrate an efficient evaluation of the hydrodynamic performance of deformed structures with a balance among low cost, high efficiency, and verifiable reliability, providing data support for the emergency decision-making of deformed ships and offshore platforms.
evidence_items.title: A fast evaluation framework for the hydrodynamic performance of deformed marine structures using artificial intelligence-based three-dimensional reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: Molybdenum (Mo) is a promising replacement for Tungsten (W) in advanced semiconductor nodes due to its low resistivity and the elimination of the need for a barrier layer. Silica particle-based acidic slurries are commonly used in the chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) process, but complete removal of these particles is critical for subsequent processes. This study investigated particle contamination and cleaning mechanisms to develop effective cleaning solutions. Mo films were polished using H 2 O 2 as an oxidizer and colloidal silica as an abrasive under varying down pressures and rotation speeds to induce contamination. Dipping cleaning for 60 seconds in de-ionized water, 2 wt% ammonia, and potassium hydroxide (KOH) solutions were performed to evaluate particle removal efficiency. High oxidizer concentration and high slurry temperature were found to result in low cleaning efficiency. Mechanical friction effects, including the rotation speeds of the carrier head and platen and the down pressure of the carrier head, were also studied. Optimal conditions of 93 rpm platen speed, 87 rpm carrier head speed, and 1 psi down pressure yielded the fewest remaining particles after cleaning.
evidence_items.title: Silica Particle Contamination and Cleaning in Molybdenum CMP

evidence_items.summary: Rigorous management of metallic contamination is crucial in microelectronics to ensure device performance. For advanced laboratories seeking to work on a wide variety of diverse projects, one challenge is, for example, to make 3D integration technology using noble metals coexist with more sensitive technologies, such as photonics. To prevent metallic cross contamination between tools, recurrent backside and bevel cleaning is mandatory throughout the process flow. The aim of the paper is to find an alternative to traditional aqua regia mixture, which is known to dissolve noble metals. For this purpose, two promising solutions for metallic contamination removal are TechniClean IK73-based and TechniClean NPS78-based solutions. The TechniClean NPS78-based solution was almost as effective as aqua regia on noble metals but introduced bromide contamination. The TechniClean IK73-based solution showed varying effectiveness depending on the metal and substrate. Silicon consumption was a key parameter for contamination removal on silicon substrates. On oxide substrates, the addition of hydrogen peroxide enhanced metal removal efficiency. Stability tests over one week and metallic loading tests showed good performance, but issues with evaporation needed to be addressed. Transferring the process to a single wafer tool is expected to optimize performance and address eco-design requirements. Further evaluation will assess the lifespan of equipment and the potential for reclaimable chemistry.
evidence_items.title: Investigate an Alternative to Aqua Regia for Backside Metal Contamination Removal

organizations: Intelligent Comprehensive Transportation Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province
evidence_items.summary: Abstract LiDAR configuration selection in roadside sensing remains constrained by limited controlled evidence across sensors. To address this gap, we present MR-LiDAR, a controlled cross-configuration benchmark comparing four LiDAR configurations from 16 to 128 beams on dynamic vehicle and vulnerable road user (VRU) targets. Its cross-configuration main set covers matched daytime, nighttime, and vehicle-occlusion conditions, while three deployment and operating condition subsets examine mounting height, target speed, and curved-road geometry. By reducing confounding from scene and trajectory variation, MR-LiDAR links sensor configuration to target point acquisition and algorithmic detection outcomes. We characterize distance-dependent point loss, define effective beam count as the number of vertical beams intersecting the target’s angular extent, and introduce a point-based Occlusion Ratio. The results show that 16- and 32-beam configurations degrade earlier with distance, while VRUs exhibit greater point sparsity than motor vehicles. Nominal beam count alone is insufficient to explain roadside scanning capability. In the cross-configuration main set, the 80- and 128-beam configurations achieve comparable results, consistent with their nearly identical downward beam layouts. A uniform 80-beam counterfactual yields only about one third of the effective beam count of the actual non-uniform configuration. Illumination and the tested speed range have little influence on target-point-count patterns, whereas mounting height and near-field road geometry can substantially alter configuration ordering. Finally, an empirical minimal-sufficient configuration matrix combines frame-level geometric sufficiency with matched-box quality and includes threshold sensitivity analysis, providing bounded configuration guidance for the tested conditions. MR-LiDAR Benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/ShunlaiC/MR-LiDAR-Benchmark .
evidence_items.title: Mr-LiDAR: a multi-resolution roadside LiDAR benchmark for perception diagnostics and deployment guidance

organizations: Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences

evidence_items.summary: Abstract In this study, we present the full (97.3% complete) 0.8–12.5 μ m spectral energy distribution (SED) of an L/T transition object, CWISE J210640.16+250729.0 (CW 2106), using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We provide a full characterization of the host star’s elemental abundances and age. We empirically derive the bolometric luminosity (≈ −4.825 dex) of CW 2106, and obtain estimates of its mass ( M ≈ 50–62 M Jup ), radius ( R ≈ 0.83–0.87 R Jup ), effective temperature ( T eff ≈ 1213 K), and surface gravity ( log g ≈ 5.28 dex). We find the near-infrared (near-IR) spectrum (0.8–2.5 μ m) is best reproduced with cloudy atmospheric models while the mid-infrared (mid-IR) spectrum (5–12.5 μ m) is best reproduced with cloudless models. This suggests a cloud layer restricted to only the deepest observable parts of the atmosphere and is qualified by the lack of a 9 μ m silicate feature. Making use of the Mg/Si ratio of the primary, alongside thermochemical models, we predict the clouds in CW 2106 to be composed primarily of enstatite (MgSiO 3 ), removing ∼23% of the bulk oxygen out of the atmosphere. Future retrieval studies will be able to help investigate the existence and full impact of these cloud species.
evidence_items.title: Sinking Silicates. I. Characterizing the Benchmark System Containing the T0 Brown Dwarf CWISEJ210640.16+250729.0 using JWST

evidence_items.summary: A comprehensive heavy metal pollution assessment of the Taloka and Wurno aquifers within the Sokoto Basin, northwestern Nigeria, was carried out. Field mapping, borehole logging and water quality analysis were integrated to describe the distribution of heavy metals in groundwater. Heavy metal evaluation points to variations between the Taloka and Wurno aquifers. A plausible hypothesis is that the dissolution of iron-rich lithologies in the Taloka aquifer contributes to the elevated iron (Fe) concentrations observed in the Taloka Formation. In contrast, redox reactions involving organic-rich shales and limestones of the overlying Dange Formation may contribute to the relatively higher concentrations of potentially toxic metals, particularly lead (Pb) and arsenic (As), observed in the Wurno Formation. The Wurno aquifer is also more vulnerable to surface contamination due to its shallower stratigraphic position. The concentrations of As and Pb in a substantial number of groundwater samples from both aquifers exceed the World Health Organization (WHO) safe limits for heavy metals in drinking water. The findings indicate a possible combined geogenic and anthropogenic influence on groundwater quality in both aquifers and highlight the need for continuous groundwater monitoring, targeted water treatment interventions and sustainable aquifer management strategies.
evidence_items.title: Heavy metal contamination assessment of the Taloka and Wurno aquifers, Sokoto Basin, northwestern Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: Cancer research generates tens of thousands of studies each year, yet whether a published finding holds in another cancer type or patient population is rarely tested, because doing so is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We define this task as discovery transfer and present SMART, a multi-agent large language model framework for discovery transfer in single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies. Given a source manuscript and a target scRNA-seq dataset, SMART extracts major clinical and mechanistic findings, generates and executes analyses for the testable findings, and reports which findings transfer and suggests follow-up. Applied to 121 studies across six cancer types, SMART identified findings that transfer across cancers, including a lung cancer prognostic signature that we confirmed to be associated with survival in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and pleural mesothelioma. SMART also generated new mechanistic hypotheses, demonstrating how agentic discovery transfer can extend published findings beyond their original setting.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Discovery Transfer Enables Cross-Cancer Discovery at Scale

evidence_items.summary: This study compares the trajectories of three artificial intelligence paradigms: generative, agentic, and quantum AI. A scientometric and technometric analysis applies linear regression and Shannon entropy to publication data and keyword-frequency corpora to measure growth, thematic breadth, and structural diversity. Empirical results show that agentic AI has the most rapid acceleration (B = 3.201, p < 0.05), despite emerging only in 2023. Quantum AI exhibits the most consistent and statistically significant growth (B = 0.70, p < 0.001), driven by advances in hardware foundations, security, and post-quantum applications. Generative AI displays a strong positive trend (B = 1.44, p < 0.001). These trajectories indicate “stack thickening” in the AI system, shifting from passive content generation toward autonomous orchestration, grounding, and multi-agent coordination. Technology policy should promote AgentOps standards, accelerate post-quantum cryptography, strengthen institutional AI literacy, support interoperable infrastructures, and establish adaptive regulation for secure, accountable, reliable, and responsible AI deployment.
evidence_items.title: The Evolution of AI Technological System: Generative, Agentic, and Quantum Paradigms

organizations: KU Leuven. Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Transplantation. Laboratory of Clinical Microbiology.;

evidence_items.summary: Background: Contact tracing is crucial to limit pathogen transmission and to gather epidemiological data. However, despite machine learning optimizations, it remains time-consuming. Large language models have been used for infection risk prediction, but no existing application converses with a user to adapt its risk estimates. Objective: We aimed to develop an iterative retrieval-augmented generation conversational framework to predict coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infection risk from textual social data. The conversational agent aims to gather personalized risk factors based on descriptions of social interactions. Methods: We trained a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to predict the risk of COVID-19 infection from 19,434 textual descriptions of social interactions, collected during the pandemic in the Leuven student community, in Belgium. We integrated this model into a Llama3.3-based conversational framework that iteratively gathers additional social information that may represent a risk of infection. We evaluated the framework using large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge metrics and by comparing its risk assessment in different social contexts. Results: Based solely on social interaction data, a fine-tuned RobBERT model predicted infection risk with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) of 0.73. It performed similarly to an LSTM model and a logistic regression on term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features, which both achieved a ROC AUC of 0.72. These three models slightly outperformed a Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA)-fine-tuned Mistral NeMo model (ROC AUC = 0.69). Llama3.3 performed well in our framework: the predicted infection risk converged often, and it asked fewer redundant questions than the smaller models (Mistral 7B, Gemma3 12B). In addition, the framework showed the ability to stratify, by risk of infection, synthetic users who had different types of social interactions.
evidence_items.title: Using iterative agentic retrieval-augmented generation to refine the risk of infection from social contexts during the COVID-19 pandemic: Development and Evaluation Study
Signaling Capability Under AI Opacity: Agentic Social Media as a Performative Arena

organizations: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The University of Aizu, Aizuwakamatsu 965-8580, Fukushima, Japan
evidence_items.summary: Agentic AI describes systems based on foundation models that extend generative AI from passive response generation toward executing tasks to achieve specific goals through planning, tool use, memory, reflection, multi-agent coordination, and environmental interaction. This scoping review maps recent peer-reviewed research on Agentic AI to clarify its conceptual foundations, application domains, technical patterns, risks, and future directions. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, searches were conducted in IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and ScienceDirect for studies published between 2017 and June 2026. A total of 3549 records were identified, 3308 records were screened after duplicate removal, and 163 included studies were synthesized. The findings show that Agentic AI is commonly operationalized through LLM or foundation model reasoning combined with multi-step task decomposition, tool or API use, RAG, memory, reflection, and multi-agent coordination. Major application areas include cybersecurity, privacy and compliance; networks and telecommunications; robotics and embodied AI; software engineering, DevOps and EDA; and knowledge, data, and multimodal analytics. A post hoc ACM Digital Library and Scopus conference-coverage sensitivity analysis showed that application-domain proportions were sensitive to database and document-type coverage, whereas the main recurring architectural signals remained qualitatively stable. Recurring technical patterns include governance middleware, collaborative and hierarchical multi-agent architectures, memory-enabled agency, executable reasoning, and closed-loop validation. Reported risks include hallucination propagation, unsafe tool use, memory poisoning, privacy leakage, prompt injection, coordination failure, cost, latency, scalability, and human-oversight challenges. Future research should prioritize real-world validation, standardized benchmarks, runtime governance, secure memory management, human oversight, and cross-domain generalization.
evidence_items.title: A Scoping Review of Agentic AI: Applications, Emerging Trends, Risks & Future Directions

organizations: University of National and World Economy Sofia Bulgaria
evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Oxygen transfer control in industrial bioreactors becomes more complex when cell metabolic changes, nonlinear process dynamics, energy constraints, and biological and operational uncertainties simultaneously affect control decisions. This study presents an innovative framework for intelligent oxygenation management that integrates a synchronized digital twin, agent‐based artificial intelligence, fuzzy‐notrosophic modeling, and multi‐objective decision‐making in a closed, uncertainty‐aware loop. The proposed framework enables predictive and safe decision‐making under variable conditions by continuously monitoring and reconstructing the process state, predicting short‐term behavior, generating and screening control options, and virtually evaluating them before implementation. Evaluation under normal operating conditions and biological and process disturbances showed that the complete framework achieved 98.04% dissolved oxygen stability and reduced the recovery time after oxygen demand shock to 7.26 min. The findings show that the main value of this architecture lies not in the single maximization of oxygen transfer, but in creating an adaptive balance between oxygen delivery, energy consumption, shear stress, biological stability, and operational risk. This framework provides an extensible platform for moving toward autonomous, resilient, and sustainable bioreactors.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence‐Driven Neutrosophic Multi‐Objective Optimization of Oxygen Transfer Systems in Smart Bioreactors

organizations: Management Department, School of Business Administration, Penn State Harrisburg, Harrisburg, PA 17057, USA
evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) changes digital retail from consumer-led search to delegated decision making, increasing both the potential value and the agency risks of recommendation. This conceptual article asks the following: Under what architectural and governance conditions can an autonomous shopping agent earn calibrated consumer trust while supporting economically and environmentally appropriate consumption decisions? Using a purposive, multidisciplinary synthesis of signaling theory, principal–agent theory, the ability–benevolence–integrity model of trust, trustworthy AI, recommender system governance, and sustainable consumption research, we develop a process model linking four architectural features to consumer perceptions, delegation, reliance, and decision outcomes. The features are scoped provenance verification, disclosed and audited commercial incentives, faithful contrastive explanations, and active evaluation of retention, repair, refurbishment, and purchase. We argue that justified non-purchase advice can function as a credible signal of consumer alignment only when the operator is the signal sender, the advice creates observable opportunity or accountability costs, and compensation and audit arrangements make imitation more costly for a misaligned operator. The framework distinguishes perceived trustworthiness from overall trust, willingness to delegate, actual reliance, recommendation appropriateness, and lifecycle sustainability. A five-layer architecture, a worked decision example, and four testable propositions specify how missing data, conflicting preferences, uncertainty, authorization, privacy, and accountability should be handled. This article treats the applications as illustrations rather than empirical cases and concludes with limitations and an empirical research agenda focused on calibrated—not merely increased—trust.
evidence_items.title: Developing Consumer Trust in Sustainable Agentic Commerce: Conditional Signals, Auditable Governance, and Justified Non-Purchase Advice

evidence_items.summary: Ladder diagram (LD) is the relay-circuit language of IEC 61131-3 in which many PLC safety interlocks are written, and model checkers built on SMT solvers do not read it. A verdict reached through a translation is only as good as that translation. We present ESBMC-PLC, which verifies LD programs with the ESBMC model checker, and argue that its translation is faithful. It encodes the scan cycle as a single loop with nondeterministic inputs, resolves graphical PLCopen XML networks into ordered rungs, models timers in milliseconds, and rejects programs outside an explicit subset. We prove, under eight stated hypotheses, that one iteration of the emitted loop agrees with one scan of a semantics for the subset, so scan-count verdicts on programs without user function blocks hold on that semantics. For timing-mode verdicts, a refinement theorem for MATIEC's timers gives evidence, not proof. One SMT query per program also compares the emitted loop with the C that MATIEC generates. On the 241 labeled LD variants of a public benchmark suite, ESBMC-PLC returns no wrong verdict against the current labels and proves 127 variants safe; ESBMC on MATIEC's C for the same programs proves 2. PLCverif with NuSMV, which shares neither our frontend nor ESBMC, agrees with ESBMC-PLC on all 207 of the 208 variants within the theorem's scope that it can run. On 413 LD programs from public GitHub repositories, none of the 104 that the per-program query can check differs from MATIEC. Every k-induction proof closes at k = 2. ESBMC's inductive step proves only properties that one scan preserves, so properties that depend on a longer history stay unproved.
evidence_items.title: ESBMC-PLC: Formal Verification of IEC 61131-3 Ladder Diagram Programs Using SMT-Based Model Checking

evidence_items.summary: Generating videos of a specific subject from a few reference images remains challenging when the camera reveals surfaces that are not visible in the input. Early subject-to-video (S2V) methods condition on a single reference image and must therefore infer the subject's unseen appearance and geometry as the viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, recent methods extend S2V to multiple reference views, providing more information about the subject from different viewpoints. However, they do not explicitly specify the 3D structure that connects these observations. In addition, existing training data do not guarantee that viewpoint changes preserve the same underlying 3D subject. We present OmniShowcase, built on two components: (i) a fully automated data synthesis pipeline that produces training videos along diverse camera trajectories, with viewpoint variation driven by underlying subject geometry, even spanning full 360-degree orbits; and (ii) a geometry-conditioning method that provides the video model with a turntable of surface-normal maps reconstructed from the reference views without requiring temporal alignment with the generated frames. We construct Showcase-4K, a corpus of 3D-asset-based videos covering twelve camera motions across 88 trajectory configurations with reconstruction-derived surface-normal conditioning, and ShowcaseBench, a held-out evaluation set with the source meshes and camera parameters used to render each video. Experiments show state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality and motion. Project page: justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase
evidence_items.title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images

evidence_items.summary: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.
evidence_items.title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty

evidence_items.summary: Producing long-form videos from narration requires interdependent decisions that remain coherent across shots. Existing agentic editors often use multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving the quality-cost trade-off of compact, task-adapted policies unclear. We address this gap with WeVisCut, a long-form script-to-video system that connects tool execution with policy learning. Its agent harness maintains shared production state so that tool feedback informs subsequent decisions and repairs. Because finished videos do not expose these decisions, our four-stage data pipeline combines editing inversion with verified replay to turn recovered editing intent into executable supervision. Applied to 3,750 finished videos, this pipeline yields over 130K training examples. We use this supervision to train a single 9B policy that coordinates production and recovers from failures within the same harness. Moreover, we introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics assessing editing quality and delivery reliability. Under a shared tool environment, WeVisCut substantially outperforms its base model and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly 33x fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. It also outperforms task-matched native editors on our proposed metrics.
evidence_items.title: WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One Agent From Narration to Long-Form Video

evidence_items.summary: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.
evidence_items.title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation

evidence_items.summary:
Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities.
  We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture.
  We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything
evidence_items.title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments

evidence_items.summary: Streaming audio-visual target speaker extraction (AVTSE) is essential for latency-sensitive applications. However, current causal systems face two coupled gaps. First, standard benchmarks fix the number of speakers at two and ignore the near-/far-field interference, reverberation, and sudden noise of real scenes. Second, high-performance causal architectures are too heavy for edge deployment. Lightweight alternatives try to reclaim capacity by repeatedly invoking a small separator, which offsets the savings. To address the first gap, we release RealSSA, a realistic AVTSE benchmark consisting of RealSSA-Sim and RealSSA-Real. RealSSA-Sim provides controllable simulated scenes with 1--5 dynamic near-field interfering speakers; scenes with far-field interference additionally include 10--15 far-field interfering speakers. RealSSA-Real provides a held-out real-recorded evaluation set. To address the second gap, we propose Falcon, a causal AVTSE method. Its Separator performs multi-scale time-frequency separation in a single encoder--decoder pass. We train Falcon with an encoder-space speaker contrastive loss. This loss suppresses near-field leakage at zero inference cost and transfers across backbones. Falcon achieves state-of-the-art extraction quality on RealSSA-Sim, LRS2-2Mix, LRS3-2Mix, and VoxCeleb2-2Mix. Compared with the causal AV-TFGridNet baseline, it cuts parameters by 91.9%, computation by 20.2 times, and GPU inference latency by 11.1 times. Code and demo are available at https://cslikai.cn/Falcon/.
evidence_items.title: Efficient Streaming Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction for Real-World Acoustic Scenes

evidence_items.summary: Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging. Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing. We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images. Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace. Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops. For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development. We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art. On a GameCraft-Bench subset, VibeGame in P2G consistently outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G with the same underlying model, including GPT-6.1-Sol.
evidence_items.title: VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promising reasoning capabilities, but reliable physical interaction requires planning that accounts for when actions are executable and how they change the world. These preconditions and effects are environment-dependent and often not captured by MLLMs, making adaptation challenging. Yet existing approaches either require costly environment-specific training or rely on unstructured interaction experience that is difficult to reuse. Therefore, we introduce CausGround, a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework that distills interaction experience into reusable action-centered causal knowledge. CausGround identifies action preconditions and effects and organizes them in a factorized world-state representation capturing object attributes and inter-object relations. At planning time, task-relevant causal dependencies are grounded in current observations to support backward reasoning over preconditions and forward reasoning over effects for action selection and multi-step planning. We evaluate CausGround on simulated high-level planning, interaction reasoning, and real-world robot manipulation. On adapted VirtualHome and RoboCasa benchmarks, CausGround improves vision-based high-level planning across MLLM backbones, increasing average task success from 24.9% to 53.3% on VirtualHome and closed-loop planning success from 43.0% to 57.0% on RoboCasa. On SWITCH, average interaction reasoning accuracy increases from 25.8% to 31.9%, indicating improved action selection, recovery, and verification. Moreover, real-world experiments show that CausGround reasons backward from MLLM-interpreted goals to derive executable high-level action sequences for sequential manipulation. These results demonstrate that reusable action preconditions and effects support long-horizon embodied planning across diverse environments without parameter updates.
evidence_items.title: CausGround: Causal Interaction Grounding for Adaptive Embodied Planning

evidence_items.summary: Realistic market impact is essential for generative limit order book (LOB) models to serve as world models for trading agents. If a simulator misprices this mechanism, agents learn policies that are optimal in the simulator but wrong in the real market. Existing metrics assess generated streams purely through distributional comparison with historical data, leaving counterfactual response to an agent's own orders largely unexplored. Here, we show that market impact emerges naturally in neural LOB generators trained solely for next-token prediction. We inject execution-style metaorders into the generated message flow of five autoregressive models across five NASDAQ stocks and measure the response using estimators from the empirical impact literature, validated on baselines whose physics is known in advance. Our benchmark evaluates any message-level generator in three phases: free generation (reading order-flow persistence against price diffusivity); metaorder injection (yielding the impact law's exponent and amplitude); and a post-execution window (measuring relaxation). In addition, comparing each visible injection to a blind, simulator-only control isolates the model's learned response from standard book mechanics. For every model on every stock, we measure how the impact responds as a function of cumulative metaorder participation. Interestingly, we observe emergent impact in generative models of market data, with exponents in the range of 0.63 to 1.21, slightly above the traditional 0.5 of the square-root law of impact. In the family of models tested, we are so far unable to observe impact decay during relaxation. We tentatively attribute this to the still-short context windows of the models. We release the benchmark as open source to validate future generative models for market data.
evidence_items.title: LOB-Impact Benchmark: Emergent Market Impact in Generative Limit Order Book Models

evidence_items.summary: People often seek advice when choosing a film, a book, or another experience whose value depends on their tastes. Large language models (LLMs) provide a convenient way to obtain such advice. We test a simple method for improving their predictions, inspired by the wisdom of the inner crowd. An LLM first predicts a person’s movie rating from that person’s past ratings. It then predicts how the general public, given the same history, would predict the same person’s rating. Averaging takes the arithmetic mean of these two responses. We evaluated 12 GPT model snapshots using MovieLens 1M. A history-size study tested 1–20 ratings for 55 users and extended the comparison to 55 ratings for 32 eligible users. Averaging improved mean squared error relative to the first response even at the longest history. A subsequent evaluation used 10 target films per person with 10 fixed history ratings. Across 320 user–movie pairs, mean squared error was 1.218 for the first response, 1.147 for the public-perspective response, and 1.150 for Averaging. Additional analyses showed that Averaging reduced errors of at least 1.5 rating points, whereas the first response produced more exact matches. These advantages did not extend to every error threshold or metric. The findings connect inner-crowd research with a simple conversational method for preference prediction and show why the choice of response should reflect the prediction objective.
evidence_items.title: Improving Large Language Model preference prediction by averaging two perspectives

evidence_items.summary: Urban next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation is fundamental to location-based services, yet accurate prediction remains challenging because user trajectories are sparse, semantically incomplete, and tightly constrained by time and geography. Recent graph and Transformer models capture transition regularities, while language model-based recommenders introduce textual knowledge, but these two lines of work remain weakly coupled: semantic priors may be plausible in language space yet infeasible under a user’s actual mobility state, and purely behavioral encoders fail to infer latent intent when observations are scarce. We introduce STELLAR, a unified state transition framework that treats language knowledge as a calibrated prior rather than an independent prediction branch. STELLAR first induces semantic mobility priors from structured trajectory descriptions, then projects them into a shared transition state and learns a feasibility gate conditioned on spatial reachability, temporal rhythm, and both short- and long-term behavioral context. A transition memory subsequently propagates this calibrated state to candidate POIs, allowing semantic evidence to influence prediction only when it is consistent with executable mobility. This design directly addresses semantic-behavioral misalignment and avoids ad hoc late fusion. Across three public check-in benchmarks, STELLAR consistently outperforms both purely behavioral and language-augmented baselines in ranking accuracy, robustness to corrupted trajectories, and cold-start generalization.
evidence_items.title: STELLAR: Large Language Model Enhanced Spatiotemporal Semantic Fusion for Urban Next POI Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Food safety sampling is a critical measure for safeguarding public health; however, current regulatory practices are challenged by fragmented risk signals, constrained inspection resources, and suboptimal inspection efficiency. To address these issues, this paper proposes a food safety sampling decision‐making method based on large language models (LLM)–guided Q‐learning. First, we leverage LLMs to extract and analyze key elements from unstructured online food safety public opinion data. This is integrated with clustering analysis and the entropy weight method to achieve quantitative risk assessment and grading. Subsequently, a food category–region risk score matrix is constructed, and the allocation of sampling frequency is formalized as a sequential decision‐making problem under resource constraints. Q‐learning is then introduced to learn optimal sampling strategies, using LLM‐generated structured heuristic values as prior guidance, thereby reducing ineffective exploration and enhancing training efficiency. Experimental results, based on data from 30 provincial administrative regions, 457 municipalities/counties, and 25 food categories, generated 4690 risk evaluation records as effective inputs for decision‐making. The results demonstrate that the derived sampling strategies align with risk priors, allocating higher sampling intensity to high‐risk food category–region combinations while maintaining coverage balance across food categories and regions. Compared to the baseline without heuristic guidance, LLM guidance significantly reduces convergence iterations while maintaining steady‐state rewards. This indicates that the proposed method accelerates policy learning without compromising long‐term returns. In conclusion, this study validates that the proposed method achieves a closed‐loop integration of risk assessment and decision optimization, providing a data‐driven methodology for intelligent food safety regulation.
evidence_items.title: A Large Language Model–Guided Q‐Learning Method for Food Safety Sampling Decision‐Making

organizations: School of Public Health, Hubei University of Medicine, Shiyan 442000, China
evidence_items.summary: Using multimodal large language model (LLMs) to generate and popularize short health-science videos can significantly shorten their production cycle. This practice plays a vital role in lowering the public’s access threshold to health knowledge and promoting the high-quality dissemination of scientific health popularization content. However, due to the limitations of creators, regulators and multimodal LLMs themselves, these generated short videos may still lead to the spread of misleading health knowledge, posing potential risks to public health cognition. Therefore, it is urgent to construct a systematic and automatic evaluation system for such health science popularization short videos. In this paper, we propose an automatic evaluation model for such short videos by leveraging the well-known Source-Channel-Recipient (SCR) framework in the field of information communication. This automatic evaluation model includes three parts: an automatic review mechanism for Source, an automatic technology-optimization mechanism for Channel, and an automatic feedback-optimization mechanism for Recipient.
evidence_items.title: An Automatic Evaluation Model for Health Science Popularization Short Videos Generated by Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming language sciences. However, their widespread deployment currently suffers from methodological fragmentation and a lack of systematic soundness. This study proposes two comprehensive methodological frame works designed to guide the strategic and responsible application of LLMs inlanguage sciences. The first method-selection framework defines and systematizes three distinct, complementary approaches, each linked toa specific research goal: (1) prompt-based interaction with general-usemodels for exploratory analysis and hypothesis generation; (2) fine tuning of open-source models for confirmatory, theory-driven investigation and high-quality data generation; and (3) extraction of contextualized embeddings for further quantitative analysis and probing of model internal mechanisms. We detail the technical implementationand inherent trade-offs of each method, supported by empirical casestudies. Based on the method-selection framework, the second systematic framework proposed provides constructed configurations that guide the practical implementation of multi-stage research pipelines based on these approaches. We then conducted a series of empirical experiments to validate our proposed framework, employing retrospective analysis, prospective application, and an expert evaluation survey. By enforcing the strategic alignment of research questions with the appropriate LLM methodology, the frameworks enable a critical paradigm shift in language science research. We believe that this systemis fundamental for ensuring reproducibility, facilitating the criticalevaluation of LLM mechanisms, and providing the structure necessaryto move traditional linguistics from ad-hoc utility to verifiable, robust science.
evidence_items.title: Systematic Framework of Application Methods for Large Language Models in Language Sciences

organizations: Nanchong Gaoping District People’s Hospital, Nanchong 637100, China

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) constitute a new growth engine for artificial intelligence, boasting tremendous potential to reshape the healthcare industry. When deploying LLMs to empower healthcare scenarios, scientific and comprehensive evaluation is an indispensable task, which can effectively mitigate potential risks and guarantee service quality. This paper elaborates on the evaluation contents and methodologies for LLMs oriented toward healthcare, and identifies key research priorities for future exploration. The work provides references for academic research and industrial practice concerning the evaluation of medical LLMs, enabling LLMs to exert greater positive impacts across the healthcare sector.
evidence_items.title: Research on Evaluation of Large Language Models for Healthcare

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND Clinicians routinely distribute printed patient education materials at the point of care. Tutorials covering all relevant information are rarely feasible within clinical time constraints and ongoing educational support is commonly needed. Patients reading these materials on their own cannot ask questions or have passages explained, and a pamphlet does not adjust to a patient’s educational needs. Embodied conversational agents (ECAs) powered by large language models could take on the role of a clinician or health educator, guiding a patient through educational materials they were given. Virtual reality (VR) additionally affords spatial grounding of anatomical references and use of attentional cues from the patient, such as gaze and pointing, as human educators do while teaching. Whether patients find such a system usable and acceptable in VR is unknown. OBJECTIVE We evaluated an agentic workflow that transforms static patient education pamphlets into structured learning sessions delivered by an ECA in VR. We conducted a formative evaluation of the usability and acceptability of the VR learning experience, including pre-post knowledge change. METHODS We conducted a mixed methods usability study. Healthy adult volunteers (N=22 enrolled; N=21 analyzed) completed a VR learning session (mean duration 18.0 minutes, SD 3.5) in which the ECA delivered a multimodal walkthrough of standardized patient education materials on colonoscopy, appendectomy, or kidney cancer, supported open-ended questions, and reinforced understanding through summaries and brief multiple-choice review questions (flashcards). Measures included overall satisfaction, perceived quality of the education material using an adapted version of the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool, pre- and post-session knowledge tests, and semi-structured interviews.
evidence_items.title: A Large Language Model-Driven Embodied Conversational Agent for Patient Education in Virtual Reality: Mixed Methods Usability Study (Preprint)

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To develop a natural-language statistical-analysis agent that integrates a local large language model, specialized medical statistical tools, and output-checking stages, and to illustrate its functionality through representative software-interface displays.Materials and Methods: MedAnalysis Studio version 1.0.1 integrates a locally quantized Qwen2-family model, named EpiMind within the application, with structured tool calls, numerical traceability checks, and methodological auditing. The system provides Chinese and English interaction. Representative single-goal operations are illustrated by preserved screenshots of missingness reporting, correlation visualization, and event categorization.Results: The system comprises 93 configured tools in 12 modules. Illustrative software screenshots show a missingness-report panel, a correlation heatmap, and an event-status display within the natural-language workflow. These examples are presented as interface demonstrations rather than quantitative validation.Conclusions: The integrated workflow connects natural-language requests with explicit statistical operations, checking stages, and structured research outputs. Representative interface displays illustrate the organization of data-quality reporting, visualization, and outcome-category handling. Broader accuracy and clinical performance require separate evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Development and Functional Demonstration of MedAnalysis Studio: A Locally Deployed Large Language Model Agent for Medical Research and Statistics Education

evidence_items.summary: Background: Severe intra-abdominal infections are a major cause of sepsis and septic shock in intensive care units (ICUs), with high mortality and heterogeneity. Identifying variables associated with mortality is essential for risk assessment in this population. The potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted analysis using large language models (LLMs) to complement conventional statistics remains underexplored. Methods: This retrospective, single-center study analyzed 172 adult ICU patients with intra-abdominal sepsis or septic shock, identified among 6674 patients over one year. Conventional statistical methods assessed mortality-related variables. Two LLMs (Google Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Sonnet 5) were separately prompted to examine the pseudonymized, outcome-labeled dataset in five runs using structured prompts; their narrative outputs were compared with conventional findings. Results: Overall in-ICU mortality was 60.5%. APACHE II showed the highest discriminatory capacity for mortality (AUC = 0.695), followed by admission lactate (AUC = 0.636) and SOFA score (AUC = 0.626). LLM outputs most consistently reproduced the direction of findings involving SOFA, APACHE II, and lactate, while coverage of other variables varied between models and runs. Conclusions: Conventional statistics and AI-assisted LLM analyses yielded largely convergent findings for mortality markers. However, variability across other findings supports AI-assisted analysis as an exploratory, complementary approach. Further validation in larger, independent, multicenter cohorts is required before widespread routine clinical application.
evidence_items.title: Bridging Large Language Model–Based AI and Conventional Statistics for Retrospective Mortality Risk Assessment in Intra-Abdominal Sepsis and Septic Shock

evidence_items.summary: This study examined the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven research methodologies on lecturers' productivity in Lagos State University (LASU), Ojo Campus. The growing integration of AI tools such as Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and ChatGPT into academic research and teaching, alongside concerns about lecturers' research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness in Nigerian universities, motivated the study. Specifically, the study sought to ascertain lecturers' awareness of AI-driven research methodologies, examine their knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT, determine their perception of these tools in enhancing research quality and academic productivity, and establish the influence of the tools on research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, with a sample of 165 lecturers drawn from seven faculties and two schools across Lagos State Owned Universities. Data were collected using a researcher-designed instrument, the Artificial Intelligence Driven Research Methodologies and Lecturers' Productivity Questionnaire (AIDRMLPQ). Out of 189 copies of the questionnaire distributed, 165 were properly completed and returned, giving a response rate of 89.2%. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) and Pearson Product Moment Correlation at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed a significant positive relationship between the adoption of AI-driven research methodologies and lecturers' research efficiency (r = 0.742), between knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT and academic productivity (r = 0.781), between lecturers' perception of AI tools and research quality (r = 0.766), and between AI tools utilisation and research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness (r = 0.754).
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Driven Research Methodologies on Lecturers’ Productivity in Lagos State Owned Universities, Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: Background: Histopathology workforce shortages and operational backlogs severely delay gastric cancer reporting. This multi-centre prospective evaluation assessed the diagnostic accuracy, clinical safety-net utility, and workflow triaging efficiency of an artificial intelligence (AI) platform for gastric biopsies across NHS Wales. Methods: A prospective cohort of 848 consecutive gastric biopsy cases across three NHS Health Boards was processed using a commercial AI platform. Diagnostic performance was evaluated against standard-of-care clinical reference diagnoses. Post-analytic cross-tabulation simulated dynamic AI-driven worklist prioritisation to quantify triage safety, false-positive alerts, and turnaround time impact across urgent and routine pathways. Results: For gastric malignancies (n = 40), the AI platform achieved a sensitivity of 100.0% (95% CI: 91.2–100.0%; AUC 0.986) and a specificity of 97.2% (95% CI: 95.8–98.1%). Sensitivities for low-grade dysplasia/adenoma (n = 12) and gastric intestinal metaplasia (n = 98) were 100.0% and 94.9%, respectively. The AI review functioned as a parallel safety net, capturing eight primary lesions missed during routine human evaluation, including one occult adenocarcinoma. In workflow simulation, the platform correctly prioritised 100.0% of cancers, including 6 cancers hidden within routine backlogs, and 97.2% (106/109) of high-risk non-cancer precursors, with false-positive alerts in 4.6% (39/848) of all cases. Conclusions: AI-assisted gastric pathology review demonstrates exceptional diagnostic accuracy, acts as a reliable clinical support tool, and enables effective risk-stratified triage. Deploying AI triage in public healthcare infrastructure offers a scalable solution with the potential to reduce diagnostic backlogs and accelerate treatment for high-risk oncology patients.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Triage and Diagnostic Support for Gastric Biopsies: A Multi-Centre Prospective Evaluation Across NHS Wales
